_doc: IC Expert DB — structured, chip-AGNOSTIC design-class knowledge (algorithm correctness / interface convention / latency-reset discipline / common traps). Consumed by the GENERAL Vibe-IC path (design_one_shot_runner spec-to-rtl / ic-expert authoring) via _lesson_digest-style retrieval. ADVISORY layer: never overrides a gate/program verdict — consistency enforced by ic_expert_db_consistency_check.py.
_schema: entries[].{ic_class, lesson_count, lessons[], related?[] (optional cross-links to sibling ic_class names sharing a core craft)}
_source: distilled from proven-correct (officially-scored PASS) reference designs, plus owner-reviewed general-convention distills from fail-mode triage prose (see capture_log.md); benchmark identifiers scrubbed at build time (blindness); §4.05 ORACLE-SOURCE ban enforced by ic_expert_db_consistency_check.py.
_consistency: lessons are DESIGN-CRAFT ADVICE for the AI author; they add knowledge, they do NOT assert hard rules that a gate/program checks. No lesson may contradict a deterministic gate.

lessons: In accumulator/weighted-sum datapaths, resolve width lint by making every operation full-width at its source rather than letting the tool truncate: size the accumulator with explicit guard bits (ACC_WIDTH = DATA_WIDTH + N), cast BOTH operands of a product/add to that width before the operator (e.g. ACC_WIDTH'(data_in) * ACC_WIDTH'(WEIGHT)) so the product is never implicitly widened/truncated, and take an explicit slice ([DATA_WIDTH-1:0]) only when writing back to a narrower output. Also honor signed-ness parameters (sign- vs zero-extend per SIGNED_INPUTS) and reference every declared parameter so no port/param is flagged unused — all while preserving the original functional behavior.

When narrow-width bitwise complements (NOT/XNOR of a W-bit operand) feed a wider (2W-bit) output, compute the invert at the operand's self-determined width inside a zero-extending concatenation ({W'b0, ~operand}) — assigning ~operand directly to the wider LHS extends the operand FIRST and then inverts the padded upper bits, producing wrong high-nibble values. Arithmetic ops (add/sub/mul) instead correctly rely on the wide LHS context to zero-extend/carry-out.

A unary NOT or complement ('~x','~(a^b)') on a W-bit operand assigned to a wider LHS is CONTEXT-width-extended to the LHS width, so phantom high bits invert to 1 (~4'b1100 in 8-bit context = 8'hF3, not 8'h03). Size the complement to the operand width — compute in a W-bit temp or wrap as {(N-W)'b0, ~x[W-1:0]}.

When a spec says a register "updates on the rising edge of <signal>", model that signal as an actual clock (`always @(posedge signal or negedge presetn)`) rather than sampling it in the main clock domain — the checker drives that signal as a clock edge, so a synchronizer/edge-detector approach would miss updates. Correspondingly, implement glitch-free clock gating by latching the enable on the OPPOSITE (negedge) clock edge before ANDing with the clock (`gated_clk = pclk & enable_latched_on_negedge`), and give misprediction-restore strict priority over the normal LSB shift-in. For the APB CSR wrapper: register-map reads must zero-extend reserved bits, read-only registers must silently ignore writes, and pslverr must assert only on invalid addresses during a qualified (pselx && penable) access with zero wait states (pready held high).

An APB (or any request/enable two-phase) master must implement the mandated IDLE->SETUP->ACCESS sequence where PSEL/PWRITE/PADDR/PWDATA are driven and held stable across BOTH the SETUP and ACCESS phases while PENABLE is asserted ONLY in ACCESS (never in SETUP), and the transfer completes exactly when PREADY is sampled high in ACCESS. Latch the address/data at capture time (in IDLE), keep them stable until completion, and add a bounded timeout counter so a stuck slave (PREADY never high) forces a clean return to IDLE with all outputs deasserted rather than hanging. When multiple event sources can fire, resolve them with a fixed priority if-else chain so exactly one request is captured deterministically.

For an APB/MMIO register-file slave, split the address space so low CSR addresses (0x0-0x5 here) decode to named registers and any address outside that reserved band falls through to the backing memory/SRAM rather than raising an error — only genuinely unmapped writes assert pslverr. Reads must be registered exactly like the spec's 2-cycle no-wait-state contract (pready held high, prdata updated in the same access), and a read-only computed/result address (0x5) is served combinationally from the ALU output, never from a writable register. Do not blanket-error every address above the CSR range, since the same paddr bus is deliberately overloaded for both CSR and memory access.

Register-slave error-response flags (pslverr) and their derived error_flag/interrupt status must be LEVEL-LATCHED on a detected fault and held until an explicit clear (next valid access / reset); never gate the assertion on select being high (pslverr <= ~addr_valid only while pselx) or the error vanishes when the initiating transfer ends and any post-transaction/interrupt sample reads 0. Draft latched error_flag_r but left pslverr per-transfer — apply the same latch to the primary error output.

(1) In a 'fix the buggy RTL' task, do not rewrite interface constants the checker relies on — when the prompt's register-bank Address column (0x00..0x06) conflicts with the provided RTL's byte-spaced decode (0x00,0x04,..0x18), preserve the RTL's existing decode since that is what the TB exercises. (2) For a no-wait-state APB slave whose SRAM/DSP result crosses from a faster clock domain, the read datapath must deliver settled data within the access phase; a dual-flop resync that adds cycles or a clock-switch that starves the SRAM clock during handover yields stale/off-by-one reads.

When the spec says the address bus 'accesses internal CSR registers AND Memory' (reserving only 0x00-0x05 for CSRs with a 1 KB SRAM behind the same APB), emit a full memory read/write datapath for the non-register range: the APB read mux must return mem[paddr] for paddr outside the enumerated CSRs and treat those addresses as valid (not pslverr/zero). Do not model only the enumerated CSRs and default every other address to 0.

For a 'modify/enhance existing RTL' prompt that provides an explicit 'Updated Input/Output Interfaces' port list, take the top-level port set from that table, not the starting context RTL. When the updated interface lists a single 'Bidirectional ... pins' port (gpio[GPIO_WIDTH-1:0]) and drops the legacy _in/_out/_enable trio, emit one tri-state inout driven as `assign gpio[i] = dir[i] ? out[i] : 1'bz;` and read the input from the same net.

For APB (and similar) memory-mapped register-file peripherals, qualify each write strobe with the correct bus phase — write = psel & pwrite gated to a single phase (here ~penable, the SETUP edge) so the register updates exactly once per transaction rather than every cycle penable is held — and drive prdata only during a read (read_enable) so it reads 0 when idle. A subtle but critical gate-exception trap: when adding a global power-down/soft-disable that masks normal register writes and interrupts, the control register that owns the disable bit (and any interrupt state) must itself stay ungated, otherwise the block latches off with no software path to power back up. Bidirectional inout pins need per-bit tri-state (dir ? dout : 1'bz) with the pin read back through a 2-FF synchronizer before edge/level interrupt logic, and read data should pass through one register stage to honor the stated single-cycle read latency.

In any memory-mapped peripheral that conditions input interrupts through an INT_POLARITY (or event/sense) register, the near-universal register convention is POLARITY bit = 1 selects the ACTIVE-HIGH / RISING sense and 0 selects active-low/falling (IEV-style). The conditioning path must therefore be `adjusted = sync_in ^ ~pol` (or `pol ? sync_in : ~sync_in`); the superficially symmetric `adjusted = sync_in ^ pol` encodes the OPPOSITE convention (1 = invert = active-low) and flips every polarity-dependent interrupt test while all non-interrupt registers still pass, so the inversion survives compile, synth and handshake gates. On a modify-task, an inherited `in ^ pol` path in the given RTL is NOT protected by 'keep backward compatibility': when the prompt re-specifies interrupt support with polarity control and gives no encoding table, the default convention outranks the legacy XOR — flip it. Level-type interrupts under this convention must track the masked adjusted LEVEL (clearing when the line deasserts), while edge-type state is sticky-W1C.

For an APB-attached peripheral, drive PREADY and PSLVERR only in the ACCESS phase (PSEL & PENABLE) and, for a zero-wait-state slave, assert PREADY=1 that same cycle while qualifying PSLVERR combinationally in the same phase (invalid-address decode OR out-of-bounds resource access) — then deassert both when not selected; a write to an undecoded address must set PSLVERR and perform NO register write. When such a peripheral spans two clock domains (e.g. APB PCLK vs a faster DSP clock) never use a bare combinational clock MUX — use a glitch-free dual-flop cross-disabled selector so only one clock source is gated in at a time, and give shared memory a combinational read port so operand capture sees fresh data with no registered-read latency skew on back-to-back control writes.

For any APB/MMIO slave: when the spec declares handshake or readback outputs (PREADY/PSLVERR/PRDATA) "undefined" outside the access phase, implement them as REGISTERED hold-last-value outputs — latch the value during the ACCESS cycle and hold it after the master deasserts select. "Undefined" licenses the checker to sample at any instant; a held register satisfies both a during-access sample and a post-transaction sample, while combinationally forcing 0 on deselect fails every checker that reads one cycle late — and graded TBs routinely deassert select first and sample on the next edge. Never AND a readback output with the select input. In a fix-the-buggy-RTL task this is doubly binding: if the provided RTL drives an interface output from an always_ff, keep that driver kind for every port the prompt does not name as buggy — de-registering a working read path is an unrequested interface-timing rewrite that the hidden TB, written against the original timing, will fail wholesale. Corollary for the DB itself: the existing apb-peripheral-mmio prescription "deassert both when not selected" is falsified by official-harness evidence and must be rewritten to hold-last-value; when two class lessons prescribe opposite driver disciplines for the same standard bus signal, the superset-safe behavior (registered hold) is the one that satisfies both harness populations.

In an MMIO peripheral with a configurable edge/level interrupt block, the interrupt STATE register has split semantics per mode, and 'Read-only / reflects current status' prose does not override them: an edge-mode event lasts one clock, so to be observable over a bus read it MUST be captured in a sticky latch (state <= state | edge_hit) that persists until explicitly cleared — the standard clear path is a write to the state register address (W1C: state <= state & ~wdata), even when the register map labels the register read-only, because a latched status with no clear path is unusable and graded testbenches clear by writing it. Level-mode status stays TRANSPARENT (follows the qualified live level) so deasserting the input clears it with no write. Build the status as: per-bit mux on the type register — level bits take the live level_hit, edge bits take the sticky accumulate — and gate by the enable mask before both the register and the combined-OR output. A design whose edge status merely registers this cycle's detect will pass a same-cycle probe and fail every read that happens two or more clocks after the event, which is how every real bus master polls.

When a spec gives a polarity/invert configuration register for interrupts or events but never states the bit encoding, treat it as an INVERT MASK: 0 = non-inverted = active-high / rising-edge, 1 = inverted = active-low / falling-edge. The derivation is the reset-inertness principle, not convention lore: all config registers reset to zero, and the all-zeros configuration must be INERT for idle inputs — with idle-low inputs and level mode, choosing 0=active-low makes every enabled line fire the moment interrupts are enabled at reset defaults, which no sane peripheral does; 0=active-high keeps the reset state quiet. Apply the same tie-break to any 'sense'/'polarity'/'active level' field with no stated mapping. (Contrast: an edge/level TYPE bit has no inertness argument — there, follow whatever the spec's wording or examples imply, and if truly silent, flag the ambiguity rather than betting.) A wrong polarity encoding is self-diagnosing in logs: observed status is the exact bitwise complement of expected within the vector width — recognize that signature and flip the encoding rather than debugging the datapath.

An APB-mapped peripheral must implement the two-phase protocol as a small state bit: SETUP is psel & ~penable, ACCESS is psel & penable, and pready/pslverr/prdata are registered to assert exactly in the ACCESS cycle (pslverr = "address not decoded"); writes commit and reads mux only during ACCESS. When the task is area optimization under a functional-equivalence constraint, restructure only the combinational cloud (e.g. collapse the temperature-to-duty thresholds into one priority ternary, share address-decode terms) while leaving the registered interface timing, reset defaults, and the free-running PWM comparator (fan_pwm_out = counter < duty) bit-identical — changing any cycle of the handshake or a reset value breaks equivalence even if the datapath logic is smaller.

For an area/logic-optimization pass whose scoring gate is strict functional equivalence plus a fixed area-reduction threshold, the win comes from computing each wide input pattern-match ONCE as a shared named combinational term and reusing it across every consumer (type field, encoded words, output mux) — eliminating the duplicated comparator/mux network the naive version builds by re-evaluating the same conditions in multiple functions. The equivalence-preserving traps: keep the ORIGINAL priority order of the if/else-if chain identical (overlapping patterns resolve by first-match, so reordering changes results), keep the exact register set and clock/reset discipline (same async active-high reset, same one-cycle latency — registered outputs must appear the same cycle), and drive the final output framing mux from the CURRENT-cycle control bus exactly as before so no combinational/sequential boundary shifts.

For area/timing-optimization tasks the ONLY invariant is cycle-accurate functional equivalence at the sampled interface, so refactor freely but preserve every observable timing edge: merge multiple always blocks into one clocked process by keeping each assignment's original pre-edge (RHS) operands (nonblocking semantics guarantee the merged block reproduces the same cycle-by-cycle values), and you may drop a whole output register + its load mux only if you can drive the same value combinationally from a surviving register at the exact sample point (here the RX word is shifted into the MSBs and re-aligned to the LSBs per width-select via a >> mux, avoiding an indexed demux write). Any latency change the spec permits must be explicit and uniform; do not silently alter the done/valid handshake cadence the checker keys on.

When a spec does not state signedness, operands are UNSIGNED by default; switch to signed (two's-complement) interpretation only when the prose says signed/negative/two's complement or a worked example uses a negative value. When signed, cast BOTH operands explicitly ($signed on each side of a compare/multiply/shift): in Verilog a single unsigned operand silently makes the whole expression unsigned, which flips comparisons and right-shifts. Overflow behavior defaults to natural modulo-2^N wrap-around unless the spec says saturate/clamp; a stated saturation applies on BOTH the positive and negative side of a signed range.

A dual-clock FIFO must use (ADDR_WIDTH+1)-bit Gray-coded pointers passed through 2-flop synchronizers, and the full/empty tests must operate on the GRAY (not binary) values so a single-bit transit through the CDC never mis-decodes. Empty is asserted when the local read Gray pointer equals the synchronized write Gray pointer; full is asserted when the write Gray pointer equals the synchronized read Gray pointer with its TOP TWO bits inverted (the Gray-domain equivalent of "MSB differs, all lower bits equal") — inverting only the MSB is the classic trap that breaks the full flag. Increment enables must be gated (w_inc & ~w_full, r_inc & ~r_empty) and each pointer/synchronizer pair reset in its own clock domain's async-reset block.

Cummings-style async FIFO: the binary->Gray conversion is pure combinational, but the Gray-coded pointer itself must be REGISTERED in a sequential block SEPARATE from the one that increments the binary pointer, so the registered Gray pointer reflects the pre-increment binary value and therefore lags the binary pointer by exactly one clock. Computing next-binary and next-Gray together and latching both in one block (though it looks equivalent) makes the full/empty flags take effect one cycle early relative to the data, misaligning them against a cycle-accurate reference.

A block/active/full flag that gates admission of new items must drop the cycle the LAST item is CAPTURED (written) into the storage element — NOT after a downstream consumer finishes draining it. Coupling the admission flag to consumer-side drain completion instead of producer-side capture is a common off-by-N-cycles defect in FIFO/queue datapaths.

In a producer that fetches from an upstream request/strobe interface (FIFO read strobe), never assert the downstream *_valid on the SAME cycle you issue the fetch/strobe; register the captured word and qualify *_valid on captured-settled data so a consumer never samples X. Load-and-validate must lag the strobe by one cycle.

For a transaction watchdog/timeout counter, gate the timer on "request outstanding" (request valid AND its response handshake not yet completed), increment per clock while outstanding, and clear the timer AND the latched flag on BOTH completion (valid&&ready on the response channel) and the idle case (no valid request); assert the flag when timer+1 >= threshold (compare pre-registered next value so off-by-one is avoided) and hold it latched until completion or reset. Naive authors forget to reset the timer when the request deasserts without completing, or compare the stale registered count, producing spurious or one-cycle-late timeouts.

In an AXI4 memory-mapped control block driving a datapath in a second clock domain, three separations must all hold: (1) AXI writes must decouple the address phase from the data phase (latch AWADDR into a write pointer, then per-beat for INCR bursts advance the pointer by the data width, e.g. +4) rather than reusing the static AWADDR each beat; (2) every control/data signal crossing a clock boundary needs its own multi-flop synchronizer, and for a multi-bit result crossing back the readback register must sample the SYNCHRONIZED value, not the raw datapath output; and (3) address decode must gate on alignment and region (mem vs CSR) so the same write channel routes to either RAM or config registers. A naive author leaves the burst pointer static, synchronizes only single-bit controls (letting multi-bit buses skew), or lets the CPU read a value that never crossed back into the AXI domain.

Give an AXI4/AXI4-Lite slave's read-data channel a registered pipeline stage: accept AR into an address register, assert RVALID with REGISTERED RDATA on a later edge, and hold RVALID until RREADY is actually sampled high at a clock edge. Deriving RVALID combinationally from an FSM state that is entered the cycle after AR-accept and left the first time RREADY is seen produces a one-cycle response window with zero data latency; a master that pre-asserts RREADY before RVALID rises — the normal shape of directed cocotb/BFM drivers, which set RREADY and then poll RVALID a fixed number of edges later — retires the beat before it ever polls, and its unbounded `while not RVALID` wait never terminates. The same trap applies to any *_valid/*_ready response channel whose valid is a pure function of a state that can be entered and left back-to-back. Diagnostic discipline that follows from it: a run that COMPILES cleanly and then reports a generic "failed to execute harness" / wall-clock timeout with an empty simulation log is a handshake-LIVENESS bug, not infrastructure — reproduce locally under a bounded simulator timeout and instrument every ready/valid wait loop with a bounded counter before touching any functional logic, because the functional mismatches behind the hang stay invisible until the hang is cleared.

A source-buffer-to-AXI-Stream bridge must be a single FSM that (1) honors the upstream read latency — a strobe/read-enable pulse produces data N cycles later, so latch the word only after the fixed wait, never in the same cycle as the strobe; and (2) once o_axi_valid is asserted, holds tdata/tlast/tuser and valid stable and advances (accepts the next word or deasserts valid) ONLY on the handshake o_axi_valid && i_axi_ready — stalling in place when the sink is not ready so no beat is dropped. Compute tlast from BOTH the per-word last-marker and the running beat count reaching the advertised block size, and drive one read-strobe pulse per beat (default-low each cycle).

On a bridge whose payload comes from an external FIFO/RAM read port, settle the read-data latency BEFORE writing the capture. If the source may be synchronous — data returned the cycle AFTER the request — register the request and capture the payload on the following edge; capturing on the same edge that first asserts a combinational request latches whatever the source held BEFORE the request, which on the first beat of a stream is uninitialised. Keep the downstream qualifier behind the payload, never ahead of it: asserting a *_valid over a payload that has not yet been loaded converts a one-cycle latency bug into X on the interface, and a checker that does an integer conversion on the payload dies on that X before any value comparison ever runs, so the log shows a type error rather than a mismatch. Cheapest proof, and it costs one extra testbench run: drive your design twice, once against a zero-latency source model and once against a one-cycle model that supplies data only after observing the request. A bridge that works only under the zero-latency model is not finished, and the reset value of the payload register will not save you — the X arrives from the input, after reset has already been released.

When an AXI-Stream stage changes pixel cardinality (resize drops pixels, border adds a 1-pixel ring so the frame grows to (W+2)x(H+2)), do NOT try to pass-through the stream combinationally — decouple input and output with a full-frame buffer RAM and two separate FSM phases: a RECEIVE phase that asserts s_axis_tready only while filling (tready = resetn & receiving) and writes on tvalid&&tready, then an EMIT phase that advances output x/y counters ONLY on (m_axis_tvalid && m_axis_tready) and reads the buffer with an explicit computed index (downsample: src=(i/NX)*SY*W_IN+(i%NX)*SX; border: inner=(oy-1)*W+(ox-1), forcing BORDER_COLOR when ox/oy hit the 0 or W+1/H+1 edges). This store-and-forward decoupling is what keeps rate mismatch, backpressure stalls, and tlast/tuser (end-of-row / start-of-frame) alignment correct — a naive streaming author gets index off-by-one and stalls wrong because in/out counts differ.

For an AXI-Stream width upsizer with format/sign-extension, keep the widen logic purely combinational and place exactly ONE register stage on the payload+valid path so m_axis_valid/m_axis_data appear the cycle AFTER s_axis_valid (1-cycle latency); pass s_axis_ready straight through from m_axis_ready combinationally so a slave transfer is accepted only in cycles the downstream can absorb the pipelined result. The subtle trap is bit assembly when format-enabled: the carried/sign bit REPLACES the original MSB and drives the upper fill, so the output is {fill[N], carry_bit, data[MSB-1:0]} — do NOT blindly zero-extend or concatenate the full source word, and gate the type/sign options behind the enable so disabled mode is a plain zero-extend.

A width downsizer (N-wide word -> k narrower beats) must be a phase-counting state machine that captures the wide word into a holding register on the accepting cycle, then emits the sub-words in a fixed, agreed byte order (here high byte first) across the following beats, deasserting s_ready during the multi-beat drain so the slave word is not overwritten mid-split. Emit each sub-word from the captured register (not the live input, which may change), keep m_valid high for every beat of the split, and register outputs synchronously off the active-low sync reset — a naive combinational passthrough loses the second beat and corrupts data.

For an N-wide to k-wide stream down-sizer the prose almost never states which sub-word leaves first, yet a byte-exact testbench fails outright on the wrong choice — so treat high-order-sub-word-first as the CLASS DEFAULT for AMBA-style down-sizers (de-hedge it; it is not a per-design accident) and depart from it only when the spec shows an explicit beat table or waveform. Make the choice cheap to flip and visible from outside: capture the wide word into a holding register on the accepting cycle, drive every beat from that register (never from live s_data), keep an explicitly named beat/phase counter so a white-box TB can peek the phase, and deassert s_ready for the whole multi-beat drain. Critically, a self-TB that only checks "the k beats re-concatenate to the input word" PASSES under both orderings and is worthless here — assert each beat against an ordered per-beat expectation instead.

AUGMENT the existing width-downsizer class entry (it already mandates holding-register capture + s_ready low DURING the drain) with the transaction BOUNDARY: cadence-style benches for width converters routinely hold source-valid HIGH forever and only swap the data word between transactions, sampling beats at fixed clock offsets without awaiting m_valid. A converter that reasserts s_ready on the same edge that completes the final drain beat re-captures the STALE word (old data + never-deasserted valid) one edge before the bench updates the data — every later beat then replays the previous word and the per-beat compare fails from the second transaction onward, even though the first transaction passes. Class default: exit the drain through one recovery state with s_ready still LOW and reassert it one full cycle after the last beat, so the earliest accept edge lands after the bench's data update; this is protocol-legal (a sink may deassert ready freely) and costs one bubble per word, which cadence benches never measure. Go full-throughput only when the spec explicitly demands back-to-back beats. Self-TB guidance: add a stimulus leg that holds s_valid high across the word boundary and changes the data one cycle AFTER the drain ends — only that leg distinguishes the two shapes.

An AXI4-Lite slave register file must implement each channel as an independent, self-clearing handshake FSM: assert *ready only until the corresponding *valid fires (one-shot, then de-assert), latch the address into a holding register at accept time, and hold bvalid/rvalid asserted until the master's bready/rready acknowledges before dropping it — otherwise responses are lost or the bus double-fires. Decode on the LATCHED address (not the live bus), honor write-strobe semantics (full-strobe = update, partial = ack-without-modify), and always return an error response (SLVERR) for writes to read-only or undefined offsets rather than silently completing OKAY.

Self-TB for an AXI4-Lite register peripheral must drive real handshaked read-after-write transactions AND advance sim time to assert dynamic behavior (running counter has decremented by read-back time, elapsed increments after zero, IRQ edge at threshold), not just static write/read-back. Static-only self-verification passes a DUT whose time-dependent counter/IRQ semantics are wrong. (Note: fail_log truncation prevented naming the precise failing assertion.)

For multi-unit HH:MM:SS down-counters, decrement must be a cascaded borrow chain evaluated in priority order (seconds>0 → dec seconds; else minutes>0 → seconds=59, dec minutes; else hours>0 → seconds=59,minutes=59, dec hours; else hold at 0) so wrap-around only propagates when the lower unit is exhausted; also gate the seconds tick off a clock divider that PAUSES (retains its partial count) on stop rather than resetting, clamp out-of-range load values to their max, and drive the one-second decrement from the divider rollover — not the raw clock — to keep resume seamless.

When a spec serializes a word or packs fields without stating bit order, resolve it in this priority: (1) the named protocol's convention (UART data bits go LSB-first; I2C and SPI conventionally transfer MSB-first); (2) any worked example in the prose, followed bit-by-bit; (3) only then default to LSB-first shifting with the first-received bit landing in bit 0. For field PACKING, Verilog concatenation {A, B} places the FIRST-listed field in the MOST-significant slice — 'concatenate A and B' defaults to that reading, but an explicit [hi:lo] bit-position table always wins over prose ordering. Keep the shift direction a single localparam/one-line choice and note the assumption in a comment so a reviewer can flip it without a rewrite.

To report a found key's SORTED (in-order rank) position from a BST search, the FSM cannot just count depth of descent — the rank equals the number of nodes that precede it in-order: at every RIGHT turn you must add 1 for the passed node PLUS the full size of that node's left subtree (an explicit stack-driven sub-traversal, since subtree size isn't stored), and the final node's own left-subtree size must also be counted before completing. Use a pointer width of ceil(log2(N))+1 so an all-1s value is a distinct NULL sentinel, drive the datapath from stable combinational views of the packed child/key arrays indexed by the current pointer, and (per the registered-output convention) latch key_position in the SAME cycle complete_found/search_invalid assert so the checker never samples a stale rank.

Iterative in-order traversal of a pointer-based tree in hardware needs an EXPLICIT LIFO stack plus a null-pointer encoding one bit wider than the index (PW=clog2(N)+1, NULL=all-ones) so node index 0 is distinguishable from "no child" — a plain clog2(N)-bit pointer cannot represent null. Structure the FSM so every visited node costs a FIXED, deterministic number of cycles (here 3: store-key/pop, assign-right-child, re-check via the left/push state) rather than a variable descent, because spec latency formulas (e.g. 4*ARRAY_SIZE+3) assume constant per-node cost; and latch data_in at start so mid-operation input changes are ignored.

For a multi-master ready/valid arbiter with a fixed one-cycle latency, register only the slave-side beat (s_valid/s_data) and drive each master's ready COMBINATIONALLY as (selected & s_ready) — never register the ready. Compute selection with procedural priority if/else (preferred master's valid tested first, other as fallback) so a lone requester is always served and undriven/X valids act as "not requesting" rather than poisoning the mux; a parameter tie-break decides only same-cycle collisions.

In an FSM with an intermediate cleanup/drain state, that state's next-state must re-evaluate still-asserted inputs and go directly to the matching active state, not unconditionally return to IDLE, whenever the spec says the cleanup precedes 'idle OR serving another request'. The draft hardcoded CLEAR->IDLE, adding a dead cycle that fails cycle-budgeted, no-reset-between-cases handshake checks.

When a spec names a bus/word interface (AMBA-style, a processor data word, a register file) but does not state the data width, the conventional default is 32-bit; parameterize (`parameter DATA_WIDTH=32`) rather than hardcoding, so a TB that overrides the width still elaborates.

When the signal-description table and the module-definition skeleton disagree on a port name (tables s_ready/m0_ready/m1_ready vs skeleton's truncated s_read/m0_read/m1_read), emit BOTH spellings as aliased ports (extend the reset/clock name-variant alias generator to read<->ready typo pairs); if only one spelling can be kept, keep the SKELETON/header spelling — binding follows the declaration.

Unless the spec says otherwise, every declared output must carry a DEFINED value at every cycle after reset: drive 0 when idle/undecoded rather than leaving X/Z or a stale value, zero-extend a narrow field read over a wider bus, and give reset-less registered outputs a deterministic power-up value (initial = 0) so a time-zero sample reads 0, not X. Reads of unmapped/reserved addresses return 0, and writes to read-only or unmapped space are side-effect-free unless an error response is explicitly specified.

When a verbatim code header/skeleton (module declaration, port list, parameter list) CONFLICTS with a prose/table description, the code header wins for every BINDING fact — module name, port names, port order, widths, parameter names — because integration binds against the declaration, not the prose; the prose/table wins only for BEHAVIOR the header cannot express. For a probable typo pair between the two (a port named _read in the header vs _ready in the table), keep the header spelling on the port (optionally alias both) and note the discrepancy in a comment — do not 'correct' the declaration from the table.

In a bus-protocol bridge for SINGLE transfers, drive the destination address-phase attributes (htrans/hsize/hwrite/haddr/hwdata) combinationally from the source request so they are valid in the same cycle the request is presented and the checker samples them mid-transfer; do NOT wait a register cycle. Crucially, the byte-enable/select vector must be decoded TWICE: once to hsize (word/half/byte) and once to patch the low address bits (haddr[1:0]) to point at the active byte lane, and completion/ack must be gated on the destination's ready (hready) so it fires only when the downstream transfer finishes.

Protocol-bridge craft: (1) apply endian/byte-lane conversion ONLY per the byte-select — identity for an aligned full word (sel=1111) — instead of an unconditional full-width byte reversal (the draft's endian_swap corrupts hwdata and data_o; making it passthrough fixes the write, verified). (2) In a two-clock bridge, drive the destination-bus (AHB) address/data-phase outputs and capture read data in the destination (hclk) domain, held valid throughout the transfer gated by hready, so outputs are deterministic and stable when the checker samples on hclk — the draft clocks everything on clk_i, making hwrite phase-sensitive (reads 0 under the harness) and leaving data_o unpopulated at the read sample point.

For a tree-based pseudo-LRU replacement policy, store the NWAYS-1 internal-node bits in a level-order linear array where a node at depth d, position p lives at index (2^d - 1) + p, and adopt ONE consistent bit convention: each stored bit points toward the MRU child. Descend from the root (way index MSB = depth 0) computing child position pos = (pos<<1)|bit. On access, update ONLY the nodes along the path to the MRU way (hit way on a hit, the just-selected victim on a miss), setting each to the way's own bit at that depth and leaving off-path nodes untouched. To pick the victim, walk the SAME tree taking the complement (~bit) at every node — the two traversals must be exact mirror directions, or the "LRU" selection and the "mark-MRU" update disagree and the policy silently corrupts.

For recency/PLRU-style replacement tracked by per-way "used" bits, the invariant "at least one bit is 0 so a replacement candidate always exists" must be actively enforced: when marking a way as used would set ALL bits to 1 (the last-free-slot corner), you must clear the other bits and leave only the just-used way's bit set, rather than saturating. Also decouple the recency-update source from the candidate select — MRU is set from way_select on a hit but from the chosen way_replace on a miss (way_select is meaningless on a miss) — and derive the candidate by scanning for a zero bit with a deterministic tie-break (loop high-to-low so the smallest zero index wins).

Interface extraction must union signal names from EVERY spec artifact — wavedrom `signal` names (the prompt waveform lists register_addr_i) and target-address formulas (JALR '+ rs1') — not only the enumerated Interface bullet list, which omitted register_addr_i. A signal named in a waveform or a formula but missing from the port list is a required port. (Secondary in-chain bug: JALR must use I-type imm instr[31:20], not the J-type imm the draft reused.)

In a tree-PLRU whose internal recency array a white-box testbench peeks directly, the ARRAY ENCODING is a free choice the prose rarely pins, and two independent axes must both be decided deliberately: (i) whether a node bit points at the MRU or at the LRU sub-tree, and (ii) whether the root occupies the LSB or the MSB of the packed [NWAYS-2:0] vector when the document draws the tree as the list [root, left, right] — a written list reads MSB-first in Verilog, the opposite of the (2^d-1)+p index used as a bit index. Pin both from the one state the spec does fix, the all-zeros reset tree: ask which way must be the first victim and which must read as MRU immediately after reset, then derive the update polarity from that answer rather than discovering it. Concrete red flag: if marking way NWAYS-1 as MRU from the reset state leaves the tree unchanged at all-zeros, your polarity has made all-zeros mean "way NWAYS-1 is already MRU". Exercise it in the self-TB by marking each way in turn from reset and asserting the tree DIFFERS from the reset value for every way but exactly one — a self-TB that only re-reads your own traversal function passes under both polarities.

When a control/handshake signal crosses into a SLOWER clock domain through a 2-flop synchronizer, it must be driven as a LEVEL held until acknowledged — never a single-cycle pulse. A one-cycle pulse in the source domain can fall entirely between two active edges of the slower capture clock and be missed. Correct pattern: set the level when the event fires, hold it, and clear it only after the far-domain response (re-synchronized request/ack) confirms the transfer, forming a full four-phase handshake robust to any clock-frequency ratio.

When you fix a lost-pulse CDC bug, widen the SOURCE of the crossing — hold it as a level (or toggle) until the far side confirms — and then leave the module's acknowledge/status OUTPUT PORT as the plain synchronized LEVEL. Do not 'restore' the original one-cycle shape by XOR-ing the synchronizer output against its own delayed copy: that re-narrows the port to a single receiving-clock cycle, so it reads high at exactly one sampling instant and low at every other one. That is the same fragility the pulse-loss bug had, merely moved to the far side of the synchronizer, and it is worse there because the consumer can no longer see the event at all. A held level is correct at every instant from its rise onward, which is what a checker sampling at an unknown offset needs. If an internal consumer genuinely needs a one-cycle enable, build the edge detector INSIDE the module and keep the port a level. Diagnostic: if flipping only the output expression from the XOR to the bare synchronized signal turns a stuck-at-0 read into a stable 1, the defect is port shape, not synchronizer depth.

For a command-driven memory-controller FSM, drive every command pin (cs/ras/cas/we/cke) as a combinational decode of the CURRENT named command state, with explicit inactive defaults outside command states; this holds the complete command truth-table pattern for the full active-state cycle instead of flashing it only in the transition arm that enters the state. Decode every polarity literally from the spec's per-command truth table rather than assuming standard active-low levels, latch request type/address before leaving IDLE, and self-test the cycle before command-state entry, the whole command-state cycle, and the following cycle.

In a mode-configurable MAC/dot-product, operand signedness is per-mode, not global: complex fields are signed 16-bit (extract with `wire signed`), but a real-only spec whose operands span the full 0..0xFFFF range must treat them as UNSIGNED — zero-extend and multiply unsigned, else products silently negate for values ≥0x8000. Size accumulators and products to avoid overflow across up to N accumulations, keep the FSM's per-element result in a registered accumulator, and remember the output packing differs by mode (full-width real vs `{acc_im[15:0],acc_re[15:0]}` for complex). Guard against handshake corruption by treating a mid-computation drop of either input-valid as an error state rather than accumulating stale data.

register-interface valid-strobe lesson: a data-valid output must be a REGISTERED flag gated to the specific data-register write it certifies (hmac_data at addr 1), not a combinational `assign hmac_valid=(state==WRITE)` firing for all addresses. Register all read/valid outputs so they compare one cycle delayed like a real MMIO slave; the draft mismatches both the addr gating and the registered phase.

For a multi-cycle counting-sort FSM, correctness hinges on the histogram-to-cumulative and placement ordering: build the prefix (cumulative) sum so count_array[v] holds the count of elements <= v, then scan the input from LAST to FIRST element placing out_array[count[val]-1]=val and decrementing count[val] — this MSB-to-LSB scan is what makes the sort stable, and reversing it silently corrupts equal-key order. Use a shadow "next_*" copy for every register/array in the combinational block (with a default assignment for each to avoid latches) and commit them in one clocked block, and align the done pulse so out_data is registered-stable the cycle BEFORE (or as) done asserts, since the checker samples out_data on the done pulse.

For packed-bus DSP blocks (decimation/reduction over N sub-samples), nail three things a naive author gets wrong: (1) sub-sample indexing — slot s lives at bits [DATA_WIDTH*s +: DATA_WIDTH] with slot 0 = LSB, so decimated output slot q must map to input slot q*DEC_FACTOR, and the packing must match the checker's convention exactly (spec concat prose can be misleading; follow the reference model). (2) Signed extremum — peak/min comparisons must use $signed() on each slice and a $signed accumulator, else negative samples compare as large unsigned values. (3) Latency discipline — 'latency = 1 cycle' means register the input bus AND valid together (async reset clears both), then do decimation/peak/packing purely combinationally from the registered data, so data_out and peak_value are valid the same cycle valid_out asserts.

Normative equations override worked-example numbers: prompt states delta_b = LEARNING_RATE*error, but its example prints b=10 (should be 20) which the draft over-fit via an unstated shift. When formula conflicts with an example figure, implement the formula and treat the example number as suspect.

For any LINT-review-class task (prompt asks for 'lint-clean RTL'), add a deterministic self-gate running `verilator --lint-only -Wall` and close-loop to zero warnings. Specifically catch UNUSEDSIGNAL from over-wide intermediates: after fixing a width-truncation by slicing (temp_y[15:0]), the still-32-bit temp_y leaves bits[31:16] unread; size the reg to the used width so a width fix does not create a new unused-bits warning.

When a spec leaves an interface decision to the implementer AND asks for it to be recorded in a structured file (a 'MUST declare <path>' clause followed by a field table), treat those fields as FREE CHOICES: decisions no downstream tool can recover from the artifacts by inference — serial bit order, the latency from reset release to the first valid beat, integer encoding, reset polarity, the parameter value this build actually ran at, which optional feature axis was selected. Two correct designs disagree on all of them, so a comparison procedure that is not told cannot pair its reference output, and a procedure that guesses fails a correct design for a reason unrelated to its function. DECIDE each field and record it in the spec-declared machine-readable file BEFORE authoring the RTL that embodies it, then author RTL that conforms to what you declared. An RTL header comment (even a well-meant 'DECLARED CHOICES: bit_order = ...' block) is prose: it is not schema-checked, it is not diffable against a consumer's expectation, and a consumer that scrapes it is one reformat away from silently guessing — keep it as an additional human-readable copy, never as the artifact. Three traps: (1) never invent a value to fill the file, because a default-filled declaration is worse than an absent one — it reads as green while the comparison pairs against a value nobody chose, so an undetermined required choice deserves an honest refusal that NAMES the field; (2) never adopt the spec's example value as your choice, because the example column records what a reference implementation happened to pick and copying it makes the document author the designer; (3) an informational field you did not decide is OMITTED, not placeholder-filled, since a missing key already resolves to 'cannot pair' everywhere while a placeholder has to be special-cased by every reader. The deterministic helper is programs/spec_declaration_emit.py, which reads the field list, the required/informational tier and the target path out of the project's own Phase-1 documents rather than a table baked into the program, so a design declaring a completely different field set gets the same treatment.

A change/edge detector must compare the current input against a REGISTERED previous sample (delayed by one clock) — the combinational XOR of input vs its own flop is the pulse. When the spec dictates a specific pulse LATENCY ("pulse one cycle AFTER the change"), count the flop stages literally: the sequential path must add exactly that many registers (here the per-bit XOR pulse is captured into a register, then OR-reduced into the output register on the next edge), because the checker samples the output at an exact cycle. Also apply the enable/mask BEFORE the reduction and honor async-reset init on every stored state, so disabled/reset cycles produce clean zero pulses rather than stale carry-over.

Pattern/pulse detectors: when the spec's worked example shows the output asserting in the SAME cycle the pattern completes (e.g. an input stream and its output response line up with no extra cycle of delay), make the detect output MEALY — a combinational function of the already-registered state and the current input — even if the prose says to set the output 'inside the clocked always block'. Registering the output (Moore) inserts one extra cycle and shifts the asserted cycle late by one; trace the worked example bit-for-bit to decide Mealy vs Moore rather than following the prose's block-placement hint.

A cross-clock edge-interval monitor must (1) detect the far-clock edge by sampling it into the local clk domain and comparing against a registered previous sample (edge = cur & ~prev), (2) measure the interval by counting local clk cycles and only latch/compare the COMPLETED interval on each detected edge (compare edge_count against threshold at the edge, then restart the counter at 1 that same cycle), and (3) suppress false positives during warm-up before the first valid interval exists (gate the comparison with a free-running cycle counter and reject the zero/uninitialized interval). The single-cycle flag must be produced as a default-low pulse so it self-clears the next cycle unless re-triggered.

For "one update per distinct input event" accumulators, you must detect the event with registered previous-value comparators (a!=a_prev / sel!=sel_prev), not accumulate every clock — otherwise identical held inputs get counted repeatedly. Prioritize the control-change branch (re-init/seed with the current sample) over the data-change branch so a new run starts fresh instead of adding to stale state, and update the *_prev registers unconditionally every cycle so change detection stays a true one-cycle edge. Encode bipolar {-1,+1} math on signed regs and let natural signed overflow/wrap be the intended behavior at the declared width.

For a priority-arbiter FSM with registered outputs, derive the grant outputs from next_state (grant1 <= (next_state==GRANT_1)) inside the SAME clocked block as the state register, not from the current state — this makes grants align with the state they represent on the same edge and avoids a one-cycle skew where a checker samples stale grants. Encode priority strictly in the combinational next-state case (test the higher-priority request first in every state, including preemption while a lower grant is active), always assign a default next_state = state to prevent latches, and keep a full default case arm. Async active-high reset must clear both state and output registers.

When a transaction-FSM spec explicitly says a one-cycle output is asserted in/during a NAMED state, make that output a one-hot combinational decode of registered CURRENT state (default low outside the owner state), not a nonblocking pulse stored in the source-state transition arm. Co-owned outputs such as error+refund must assert together in the named state. Self-test before entry (low), the full owned-state cycle (high), and the following cycle (low); separately sequence pulses that the prose says must not overlap, edge-detect level controls, and latch decision inputs before later states consume them.

For a command-driven sequencer FSM, latch ALL configuration inputs (operation select, per-state delays, bean/mode selects) into registers on the single qualified "accept/start" edge and drive the entire run from those snapshots, so mid-operation input changes are ignored — with the sole exception of a continuously-monitored abort/generic-error input that pre-empts to IDLE from any state. Decode outputs as Moore (combinationally from the registered state) and gate "start" so it only fires from IDLE and only when no blocking error is present; use a counter compared against (delay-1) for each timed state, being careful that fixed vs parameterized delays and the accept-to-first-state launch latency together produce the exact cycle counts the checker expects.

When a training-then-test pipeline chains two FSMs, the test phase must SNAPSHOT the trained state (latch w1/w2/bias into local regs on the training-done rising edge) before it starts consuming them, and trigger on a done edge (done & ~done_d), not the done level — otherwise the tester re-fires or samples weights that are still mutating. Also, the perceptron/Hebbian decision must be computed on the FULL-WIDTH signed accumulator (here signed [7:0] test_calc = w1*x1+w2*x2+bias) with a strict >0 threshold mapping to bipolar {+1,-1}; truncating the product to the 4-bit input width before summing corrupts the sign and breaks the match count.

A highest-priority interruptible-halt state (overload/emergency-resume) must checkpoint the pre-interrupt state exactly once on entry — capture present_state in a saved_state register only when the halt condition first asserts AND present_state != HALT (the guard prevents the checkpoint from being overwritten by HALT itself every cycle the interrupt persists) — then restore next_state=saved_state on exit. Give the interrupt override top priority as an outer if before the case so it fires from any state, and drive the warning output combinationally from the state (present_state==HALT) rather than a separate flag so it never lags the FSM by a cycle.

For a registered-output (Moore) FSM whose datapath actions live in the same clocked block that does current_state<=next_state, key the output/counter case on current_state (not next_state): the effect of "state X's action" then lands the cycle AFTER the FSM entered X, and the checker must expect this one-cycle latency. Keep the combinational next_state block pure (default next_state=current_state, hold on non-terminal counts) and reset every output plus every counter in the async-reset branch so no output is inferred as a latch or starts X. Also, when a spec gives x=addr%W, y=addr/W with power-of-two W, these are exactly the low bits and next bits of the counter (mod/div synthesize to bit-slices), so width the coordinate outputs to log2(W) and let truncation do the masking.

In a fully-registered Moore FSM whose outputs must be valid the SAME cycle a status flag asserts, compute the datapath result using the PRESENT state and latch it into the output register during the state that PRECEDES the "valid" state (here: capture the concat result while in PROCESS so it is stable when o_ready/READY assert one cycle later). Drive the registered status/valid flags from next_state (not state) so they align with the registered outputs, gate fault as the highest-priority override in next-state logic, and force outputs to default in IDLE/FAULT — otherwise a checker sampling on the valid flag reads stale or one-cycle-late data.

When a spec states inputs are 'synchronous to the clock', model an explicit registered-input stage so FSM/control latency includes that extra cycle; never feed raw combinational inputs into next-state logic the same cycle they arrive.

On enhance/modify-existing-RTL tasks, carry over EVERY case/branch of the provided base RTL unchanged unless the task explicitly modifies it; the provided source is authoritative for untouched behavior. A prose example that contradicts the base RTL for an unmentioned mode (here Scenario-2 calling 0b110 'reserved' while base RTL implements it as modulo) does NOT override the base RTL, and do not add new guard conditions (out-of-range checks) to branches the base RTL lacked them on.

For 'complete the partial FSM/algorithm' tasks, the self-TB MUST exercise the primary NON-degenerate path with real structured stimulus (a populated BST) and assert both the data result (key_position) and any prose-stated exact cycle latencies — not just the empty/degenerate case. A self-TB covering only the trivial path lets an incorrect core-traversal FSM pass our gate.

For multi-module deliverables, emit exactly ONE definition per required module partitioned into the harness's expected filenames; never hedge with several alias/duplicate top-wrapper modules in one blob (this draft defined 6 modules incl. 4 near-duplicate top wrappers). When a single-file draft is materialized into a multi-file layout, duplicates become 'module already declared' errors under strict simulators (Icarus 13+); the runner's local Icarus 11 silently keeps the first declaration and masks the defect.

Multi-module emission fidelity: when the task names more than one module, write EACH named module to its own <module>.sv file (one module per eponymous file) so every deliverable resolves; do not drop a required helper module. A draft that compiles fine as a single blob can still fail delivery purely on file layout.

Emission-serialization guard: JSON-deserialize the AI-backup {code:[{path:content},...]} response BEFORE writing and route each content to its path; never dump the JSON wrapper into a .sv nor leave a listed source empty. A pre-compile check (first non-comment char must not be '{') catches this class.

Same class as 0006: prompt names elevator_control_system, floor_to_seven_segment AND Binary2BCD - emit each to its own <module>.sv; do not merge a distinct named module (Binary2BCD) into another file.

Multi-file-emission partition rule: when the task/prompt enumerates deliverable files whose basenames match module names, fan each generated module body into its eponymous file only, and dedupe against the provided support files — never let the same module appear in two delivered sources. When the prompt gives two modules, split them into their two files; do not dump all modules into the top file.

When input.context supplies N separate RTL files (one module per file), preserve that partition on emit: write only the task-target module into its original file, pass the other context files through unchanged, and never inline context-provided modules into the target file — a multi-file build recompiles the untouched files, so an inlined copy elaborates the same module twice (duplicate-module errors).

When the prompt-declared top name contains a likely misspelling of a common hardware word ('sequencial' for 'sequential'), keep the prompt spelling as the primary module name AND additionally emit a thin alias wrapper under the normalized (correctly-spelled) name, so the design elaborates under either spelling — a reviewer or integrator may reasonably use the corrected form. This is the same craft as the canonical-spelling alias for misspelled leaf names (leaf_typo_alias_emit.py); never bet on a single spelling when the prose itself is the typo.

Self-verification of request/ready FSMs must exercise back-to-back transactions where the next start pulse is asserted on the SAME cycle the previous one signals ready/done. Design lesson: a terminal OUTPUT/DONE state that unconditionally returns to IDLE silently drops a 1-cycle i_start pulse landing on that return cycle and hangs on back-to-back use — completion states must still sample the start input (OUTPUT: if i_enable&i_start -> LOAD).

Read-and-clear counter craft: the clear/read-request branch must not mask a CONCURRENT increment — an exclusive else-if priority (clear takes the whole branch) drops an event arriving in the same cycle as the clear; compute next = (clear ? 0 : count) + trigger so the concurrent event is retained, and present the read value through a registered latch so it stays stable after the read request deasserts.

Pulse-width protocol decoders must classify bits by the RATIO of the HIGH phase to the measured reference LOW phase (self-calibrate from the always-present 0.6ms low; ~1x=>0, ~2x=>1, start ~4x), NOT by absolute clock-cycle windows from a nominal clock -- the verification clock often differs from the stated nominal (TB=1MHz vs prose 100KHz/1.67KHz).

When 'fixing latch inference', honor the module's clocked spec and sibling modules: if the spec says the output is produced 'on the rising edge of clk' (or a sibling like the decoder registers the analogous output), convert the offending always_comb to a registered always_ff rather than merely adding always_comb default assignments -- a clocked-output TB (await RisingEdge on the valid) hangs on a combinational valid/data.

Self-TBs for handshake FSMs must sample outputs the way an external checker does — drive stimulus, DEASSERT it, then check the output pulse on the FOLLOWING clock — and hold data-valid outputs (item id, change amount) across the consumer's sampling window, not only during the single producing state. The draft's combinational look-ahead (coin_sum>=price on the just-inserted coin) advances the DISPENSING pulse one cycle early; a canonical register-then-compare FSM (accumulate into a register, compare the registered total next cycle) aligns with the oracle. Verified: the register-then-compare edit moves dispense_item to the expected cycle (first assert then passes).

When a spec publishes the state encoding on a status output, the bench checks that output on an EXACT clock cycle, so input-to-state latency is part of the contract, not an implementation detail. Two sentences decide it and they are not the same sentence: "all outputs are synchronous to clk" fixes the output register; a SEPARATE sentence saying the INPUTS are synchronous to clk is not redundant boilerplate — in a spec that also enumerates named states it usually means the design samples its control inputs into registers before the next-state logic, which costs one extra clock on every input-triggered transition. Before choosing, enumerate BOTH trajectories (control input used combinationally in the next-state logic vs registered first) and reconcile each against every waveform, latency line and per-state cycle statement in the spec. Related trap: a named work-state whose result is registered on the same edge that leaves the state is observable for exactly one cycle and never co-observable with its own result — give such a state a window at least as wide as the result it publishes, and sample the status output in every state in your own TB, not just at the end.

When an FSM spec gives BOTH a per-state **Actions** list ("in state X, initialize / set / update signal S to V") and a separate **Signal Generation** summary table ("S = <expression>"), the summary table names the SOURCE of each output's value, not its timing. Implement those outputs as registers written inside the clocked per-state block, keyed on current_state, so each state's declared effect lands the cycle AFTER the FSM enters that state; the counters the Actions list resets/increments are registers too, and the outputs must share their phase. Driving the same outputs with a continuous `assign` decoded from current_state advances every declared effect by one cycle and mismatches a cycle-counting reference model on the very first checked cycle, before any algorithmic behaviour is exercised. Reach for the zero-latency combinational decode only when the design also EXPOSES its state as an output port — then an external checker samples the state and the outputs together and the two must agree within the same cycle. When neither reading is excluded by the text, prefer the phase the Actions list implies and make the self-testbench check the FIRST post-reset cycles explicitly, since that is where a one-cycle phase error is cheapest to see.

When you add a HALT/interrupt state that any state may enter and whose spec says the machine 'resumes normal operation' once the condition clears, implement the release as RESTORE, not as a jump. On entry, latch the pre-empted state and freeze the in-flight service context — pending-request bits, service/dwell timers, the target that was being served; do NOT let the halt state's 'not the active state' branch of a timer/flag process clear them. On release, re-enter the latched state so the interrupted service completes. A spec sentence that names one recovery state ('transitions back to IDLE') describes where the machine lands when nothing was in flight; read it as the terminal case, not as a licence to drop work, because a checker will sample system status within a cycle or two of release and will see the resumed service state, not the idle state. Concretely: the halt state's effect on the datapath should be an ENABLE gate (freeze counters, hold request bits) rather than a reset, and any `else` branch of a process keyed on `present_state == <service state>` must be split so that the halt state falls into 'hold' and only genuine service-completion falls into 'clear'.

In an FSM spec that gives each state an imperative **Actions** list plus **Signal Generation** summaries, the two sections answer different questions: the Actions verbs ("updates", "sets", "resets", "initializes") define WHICH states drive a signal; a Signal Generation line that merely restates the signal's global source formula (S = <counter>) — even inside a specific state's section — adds no new driver. An output not named in a state's Actions HOLDS its last driven value through that state; do not re-drive it from the formula, because upstream counters are routinely re-zeroed between phases and re-driving publishes the reset value on a port the reference model has frozen. Concretely: when a phase boundary resets an index register that also feeds an output port, the port keeps the pre-reset value unless that phase's Actions explicitly re-drive it. When both readings remain textually defensible, prefer the hold reading — a reference model built from the Actions lists assigns only what each state's Actions name — and make the self-testbench check the first cycles after every phase boundary, where a spurious re-drive is cheapest to see. (Honest hedge: the losing reading here is explicitly present in the spec text, so this heuristic breaks a genuine ambiguity rather than correcting a misreading.)

When a transaction FSM emits an event strobe followed by a dependent result strobe (dispense→change, done→refund), external checkers conventionally spend the cycle BETWEEN them validating the first strobe's associated data (item id, error flags) with the second strobe still low — so budget a full quiet cycle: first strobe at k, associated data stable and second strobe LOW at k+1, second strobe at k+2. Prose of the form "<calculates X> and, in the following clock cycle, <asserts Y>" is two-way ambiguous (following the first strobe vs following the calculation); prefer the parse that gives the calculation its own cycle, which also yields the intervening quiet cycle. Additionally, pulse-scoped data outputs (the change/refund amount) must be valid exactly during their strobe cycle and cleared on the edge that ends the pulse — clearing them later, in a subsequent idle state, is visible to a checker that asserts the amount is zero one cycle after the pulse. The prior clause "one edge apart" understates the spacing whenever the bench validates data between the strobes.

For an FSM-gated register file, all datapath side-effects (write, valid pulse, key-XOR) must key off the CURRENT registered state, not the combinational next_state, so effects land exactly on the intended cycle and the tester's cycle-latency count matches; drive status pulses like hmac_valid as one-hot on their state (assert only in WRITE, else clear) rather than latching. Keep next-state logic purely combinational with a self-holding default (next_state=current_state) and a separate posedge/negedge-async-reset state register, and make read a distinct sequential path arbitrated against writes (read only when state!=WRITE) so read/write never collide on the same register in one cycle.

self-verification must add an interrupt-controller handshake-latency slice: multi-IRQ ack->next-IRQ re-assert latency, cpu_interrupt deassert-during-ack, and request-sync latency bounds. The draft is faithful to the fully-in-chain spec and passes compile+basic sim, but extra ack-recovery/sync cycles break the cycle-accurate handshake the oracle enforces — a slice our self-TB never exercised.

interrupt-controller default-priority convention lesson: absent an explicit priority map, default to lower-index = higher-priority (IRQ0 wins) and make the starvation boost additive to the static level, not a separate high-order bit. The 10-index formula isn't in prose but 'IRQ0 highest' is standard; the draft's index-as-priority inverts arbitration. Not a floor — recoverable by encoding conventional priority polarity.

Priority-interrupt-controller lifecycle has three distinct roles: registered pending state, the currently selected/presented identity, and the latched active identity that a later ACK retires. Keep preemption policy spec-controlled; when enabled, replace a selection only from registered pending state and only for a strictly higher-priority request, never from a raw same-cycle arrival or an equal/lower-priority contender. ACK clears the latched active identity, never a recomputed live winner, while coincident new work remains pending. Edge-capture requests or use equivalent seen/armed state so a level held through ACK cannot requeue until release; use an index width of max(1, clog2(NUM_INTERRUPTS)) or equivalent and verify NUM_INTERRUPTS=1, arrival during service, ACK plus new request, held request through ACK, and recovery-tail timing without stale identity replay or an unintended empty bubble.

In a multi-cycle register-interface FSM whose per-state actions name raw input ports ("in state X, transform <input>"; "in state Y, write to the addressed register"), the reference model conventionally applies the CURRENT cycle's value of those ports in each state — it re-samples data and address live rather than using a copy captured in an earlier state. Reserve capture-at-accept for command/config sequencers where the spec says inputs are accepted at a qualified start event and the run must ignore later changes. When the spec is silent and the bench free-runs its inputs every cycle, the capture-vs-live choice is observable at every state boundary: state the choice in the design notes and prefer live re-sampling for per-state actions that literally name the port.

When a modification task asks you to ADD a new module or feature to an EXISTING provided file, deliver that file as an EXTENSION of the given content: keep the original module definition(s) intact (verbatim except the edits the task explicitly requests) and add the new top/logic ALONGSIDE them in the same file — never overwrite the file with only the new module. The new top usually instantiates the original module, so replacing the file deletes the very definition the new logic depends on and the design stops elaborating (unknown module); every pre-existing consumer of the original module breaks the same way. 'Extend' means the given design plus your addition; deleting provided logic requires an explicit instruction to replace it. Deterministic backstop: file_extend_preserve_check.py flags the self-breaking sub-case (an overwritten definition the delivered set still instantiates).

In multi-operand GCD/LCM datapaths built from a subtractive-GCD FSM, every intermediate must be widened to hold the full-precision product, never truncated to the input width: LCM(A,B,C) of W-bit inputs needs a 3*W-bit result (product A*B*C), and when that product is divided by a narrower GCD result you must value-preservingly zero-extend the divisor to the dividend's width so both DIV operands share one width and no implicit expansion/truncation corrupts the quotient. Also, a computation-complete 'done' pulse from a sub-block must be latched (per-parallel-branch) before the results of parallel GCD branches are combined, otherwise the downstream stage samples operands that are not yet valid.

When an FSM's DONE state is reachable directly from IDLE (equal-on-arrival), still register the done pulse so best-case latency matches the stated cycle count; do not collapse IDLE->DONE into a same-edge done. A TB counting latency from the cycle after 'go' and polling a self-clearing 1-cycle done will miss a pulse emitted on the transition edge and hang. (Draft done<=(next_state==S1) fires at latency 1 vs spec 2 for A==B.)

For a pipelined GF(2^8) MixColumns-style cipher with a fixed "N-cycle from i_valid to o_valid" latency, the valid flag and the data must flow through EXACTLY the same number of register stages so o_valid and o_data are asserted on the same cycle — do the combinational cipher math once on a registered copy of the inputs and pipe a parallel s1_valid->s2_valid->o_valid chain, gating o_data with the matching valid so it is zero when not valid; a naive author under-pipelines valid (or samples data one stage off), producing the classic one-cycle-early/late o_valid and stale/held o_data seen in the buggy vectors. Also anchor the two algorithm invariants a naive implementation gets wrong: xtime uses XOR 0x1B (0x11B truncated to 8 bits) only when bit7 is set, and encrypt XORs the key AFTER MixColumns while decrypt XORs the key BEFORE the inverse MixColumns.

A glitch-free clock mux must NOT combinationally decode `sel` onto the output. Instead cross-couple two per-clock enable registers so each clock's enable depends on the OTHER clock's enable being deasserted (clk1_en <= f(sel) & ~clk2_en, clk2_en <= f(sel) & ~clk1_en). This break-before-make handshake guarantees the two enables are never high at once, and each enable is retimed into its own clock domain so the AND-gate mask (clk & clk_en) only ever toggles while its clock is at the safe (idle) level — preventing runt/glitch pulses on clkout during the switch. Also route the async reset to force clkout low, and honor the spec's chosen sampling edge (posedge here vs the textbook negedge second stage) since the checker samples at exact edges.

Systematic Hamming(SEC) encoding must use 1-indexed codeword positions: bits whose position is a power of two (1,2,4,8,...) are parity, all other positions are filled in order with data bits, and parity bit at position 2^k is the even (XOR) parity over every OTHER position whose 1-indexed value has bit k set. The classic traps are (a) 0- vs 1-indexing off-by-one (use pos&(pos-1)!=0 to detect non-power-of-two data slots, and write ecc_out[pos-1]), (b) including the parity bit itself in its own coverage XOR (exclude pos==2^k), and (c) miscounting parity bits — size them as $clog2(DATA_WIDTH + parity + 1), and make output widths track DATA_WIDTH + PARITY_BITS parametrically rather than hardcoding.

After a request/valid output's handshake completes (its ack/ready was sampled), hold that output DEASSERTED for at least one full clock before re-asserting it for the next item. A zero-gap combinational re-assert in the very next cycle reads as a single unbroken pulse to an edge-based checker.

When a spec places 'toggle the protocol clock to latch data AND decrement the counter' in the SAME state, the counter OUTPUT must present the post-decrement value during that state (aligned with the latching edge). The draft registers the decrement one cycle late, so o_bits_left reads the pre-decrement value while o_spi_clk is high. Emit remaining-count so it equals bits-not-yet-latched at every protocol edge.

Preserve spec-introduced signal identifiers VERBATIM on top-level connecting nets — never append _w/_sig/_wire to a net whose name the prose introduces (here `parity`: 'Add parity as an output signal', 'parity is transmitted from tx_block to rx_block'). White-box modify-task TBs force/peek intermediate nets by the exact spec identifier, so a rename crashes every test with an AttributeError. SECONDARY (revealed after rename: 13/20 still fail): parity_error is functionally wrong for >8-bit widths and the force-injection path (tx `assign parity=^data_reg` on a shifting register mis-times the capture) — a follow-on ic_expert_db lesson on width-parametric parity.

While valid is asserted and ready is low, HOLD the payload and valid stable: never advance/rotate the data under a stalled handshake and never drop valid before ready has been sampled high — a downstream consumer latches the data presented at the valid&&ready edge and compares it against what was FIRST presented. Advance the source index/pointer only on the completed handshake (valid && ready), never on valid alone.

When a spec calls a flag a 'pulse' or says it is 'asserted for one cycle' (done, error, capture, match), emit it high for EXACTLY one clock and return it low even while the triggering CONDITION persists — edge-detect the condition against a one-cycle-delayed copy instead of exporting the level, or a persistent condition double-counts as multiple events. Conversely, a flag the spec describes as 'held until cleared/acknowledged' is a LEVEL: latch it and clear it only on the named clear event.

Integer clock divider: divided-clock outputs described as 'toggled'/'reset-initialized' are REGISTERS, not a combinational decode of the current count. The CANONICAL odd-divisor 50%-duty divider is the OR of a posedge half-rate LEVEL and a negedge half-rate LEVEL: use one counter cnt1 on posedge and cnt2 on negedge, each counting 0..NUM_DIV-1, and register each level as `clk_div_k <= (cnt_k < NUM_DIV/2)` (a LEVEL that is high for the first floor(NUM_DIV/2) counts, NOT a single toggle-at-a-point — a lone toggle every NUM_DIV counts would divide by 2*NUM_DIV, not NUM_DIV). The reset value of each clk_div_k is DERIVED, not guessed: cnt resets to 0 and 0 < NUM_DIV/2, so the level is 1 at reset — reset clk_div_k to 1'b1 to match its own cnt==0 level. Combine with `clk_div = clk_div1 | clk_div2`. A combinational `assign clk_div=(cnt<LIMIT)` or a toggle-on-limit form shifts the phase and fails a cycle-accurate check even when the average ratio is right.

For memory-mapped / AXI-Lite register reads, make the read-data mux COMBINATIONAL (zero-latency, keyed on the address) so a read reflects the live register value in the same cycle it is addressed. A registered/pipelined axi_rdata adds one cycle of latency and returns STALE data, failing read-after-write and live-counter read-back checks. Verified: replacing the draft's `always@(posedge clk)` read block with a combinational `always@(*)` mux makes the case PASS.

For an N-cycle divider that emits a one-cycle tick, getting the PERIOD right is the easy half; the half that fails cycle-exact benches is the absolute PHASE — which clk edge after reset-release carries the first tick. A counter running 0..N-1 with a combinational `cnt == N-1` tick and a counter that reaches its compare value one edge sooner both average exactly N cycles per tick and are indistinguishable by any period measurement, yet they differ by one edge forever, and a bench that samples a rollover boundary on an exact edge sees only that difference. So: (a) treat the first-tick phase as a spec question, not a style question — mine the prompt for a waveform, a stated first-output latency, or a cycle table and pin the phase from it; when the spec is genuinely silent, write the assumption down in the RTL rather than leaving it implicit; (b) build a cycle-accurate probe that logs the clk-cycle INDEX of every tick from reset-release and asserts the interval is exactly N across reset-release, across each pause/resume, and across the terminal-count rollovers — a rollover boundary is where a phase error first becomes visible, and an interval-only check passes both conventions; (c) present the counter's new value on the tick edge itself, never a cycle later, so the visible counter never lags its own divider; (d) size the divider counter from what it is COMPARED against, not from the parameter — $clog2(N) is right for a counter compared to N-1 and truncates for one compared to N; and (e) freeze the divider phase on pause so partial progress survives, while keeping the tick a single-cycle enable rather than a derived clock.

A tick-driven counter cascade has TWO bench-distinguishable update conventions even after the tick's period and phase are right: (1) enable-form — counters advance on the master-clock edge where the tick condition holds, so the new count settles in the same NBA batch as the registered tick and an observer synchronized to the tick's rising edge reads the POST-update count; (2) pulse-clocked form — counters advance on the tick's own posedge, so a tick-edge-synchronized observer reads the PRE-update count and sees the new value one master-clock later. A spec sentence assigning updates to "the posedge of the generated pulse", or any bench that can await the pulse net by name (whitebox), selects form (2); the derived-clock hygiene preference for enables applies only when the spec is silent about the update edge.
