The discriminating probes are an expected-count read AT the pulse edge (form 1 reads i, form 2 reads i-1) and a rollover read one master-clock after the terminal-value pulse (form 1 still shows the terminal value there).

For iterative fixed-point update datapaths (SGD/DSP accumulators), compute each intermediate (product, error, delta) in a full-width signed register wide enough to never overflow (per the spec's derived widths), but let the final state register assignment IMPLICITLY TRUNCATE the wide sum to its DATA_WIDTH low bits — i.e. w_reg <= w_reg + delta_w where the RHS is wider than DATA_WIDTH. The trap: forcing everything to DATA_WIDTH early (losing precision mid-computation) or, conversely, saturating/sign-extending the final store instead of taking LSBs. The reference model's bit-limit is a wrap/mod-2^W truncation, matched by SystemVerilog's natural narrow-target assignment, and every operand/localparam must be declared signed so the multiplies are signed.

A bit-serial restoring divider needs a (WIDTH+1)-bit partial-remainder register: each iteration shift-left-brings-in-the-next-dividend-MSB then trial-subtract the zero-extended divisor, and use the extra MSB (sign/borrow bit) of the subtraction to decide — if 0 the divisor fits so keep the difference and set quotient bit 1, if 1 restore the pre-subtract value and set quotient bit 0. The quotient is built by shifting in that fit-bit each cycle. Two traps to avoid: (1) doing the width comparison on only WIDTH bits loses the borrow-out that signals "does not fit"; (2) the datapath is combinational but the result register/valid strobe are updated on the SAME final iteration (cnt==WIDTH-1) using the combinational rem_next/quot_next, so the checker sampling on valid sees fresh data rather than a stale registered copy one cycle late.

For a multi-cycle iterative sorter (odd-even/brick sort) that does one compare-and-swap per cycle, the total latency the checker expects is fixed and must be hit exactly: use a dedicated FSM (IDLE→LOAD→SORT→DONE) with two counters — a pass counter run for exactly N passes and a pair counter that walks N/2 pairs on even passes but N/2−1 on odd passes (odd-pass base index = 2*pair_idx+1). Advance pass_cnt only when pair_idx reaches the last pair, keep the compare-and-swap in non-blocking assignments so both array cells swap atomically, drive out_data and pulse done for exactly one cycle in the terminal state, and guard empty passes for small N. Getting the per-pass pair count or the fixed +constant cycle overhead wrong makes the checker sample stale/mistimed data even when the sort algorithm itself is correct.

For iterative weight-update trainers (Hebbian / perceptron / Fausett-style), the convergence/stop criterion is that the weight DELTAS are all zero on a pass — not that two consecutive weight snapshots happen to be equal. Test the update magnitude, not snapshot equality, or a coincidental repeat halts training early.

Microcode/FSM lesson: a microinstruction spec'd as 'signal stop and branch, no change to other signals' must NOT clobber accumulated datapath regs (draft's action-4 zeroes weights on stop; spec says retain), and accumulator state must live in sequential regs, not an always_comb block that reads/writes its own outputs (combinational feedback = no cross-cycle retention). Honor each action's explicit 'other signals unchanged' contract.

When a spec says to EXTEND an existing microcode-ROM state machine with a new phase (e.g. a post-training test loop), implement it as additional ROM states advanced one-microinstruction-per-clock so per-step outputs stay observable at the same cadence as the existing phase; do NOT collapse it into a single-cycle combinational sweep that races to 'done' and only leaves the final result visible.

A convergence/stop flag must be TERMINAL: once raised, freeze both the sequencer and the trained registers until reset. The specific trap is the BRANCH TARGET — a microcode spec that says 'signal a stop condition and move to address 0' does not authorize re-EXECUTING address 0's initialization action; if the address register keeps stepping, that init microinstruction re-zeroes the converged weights and the next stimulus starts an unwanted second training pass, so the checker reads garbage even though the design converged correctly. Gate BOTH the address update and the action decode on !stop, and make stop sticky. Recognize it in a waveform before blaming the learning rule: the correct converged values appear, the stop flag pulses, and then the values are destroyed later in the same run — that is a halt-discipline bug, not a convergence-criterion bug, and re-tuning the stop criterion will not fix it. Corollary: the value a checker reads at the END of the run is the only one that counts, so any state the design still owns after the stop must be read-only.

When an iterative trainer/search datapath is verified by a testbench that applies stimulus on a fixed clock cadence (one vector per loop pass, no handshake), every pass through the control loop must consume exactly one stimulus slot — the loop's cycle count is part of the contract even though no spec sentence states it. Two disciplines follow: (1) an iteration counter whose spec declares a value domain ('takes values 0..N-1') must wrap modulo N at the increment site itself; parking the wrap in a separate recovery state lets the counter transiently leave its domain and inserts a dead pass with a null selection. (2) A dead pass is invisible in the first epoch — outputs still match the worked example — and first corrupts results at the wrap boundary, where the design starts pairing stimulus k with the selection for k-1; so hand-trace one full wrap boundary against the worked example before trusting a first-epoch match. Symptom signature: convergence to plausible-but-wrong values with the done/stop flag still correctly asserted at the checker's read time — a cadence bug, not a learning-rule bug.

To extract a data-dependent bit window (mantissa) at the leading set-bit of a vector, use a variable indexed part-select with a RUNTIME base and CONSTANT width — `num_i[(base) -: 12]` — never a `[hi:lo]` slice with variable bounds (illegal). Ensure the base-index arithmetic is wide enough to hold the max index (here `exp_bin + 5'd11`, sized to 5 bits) so it does not truncate and mis-address the window. Priority-encode the leading-one by looping ascending and letting the LAST matching write win (highest index survives), and remember the position index vs. the count-based exponent differ by one — the `+1` correction and the explicit all-zeros special case are both required for correctness.

An RS/CRC-style shift-register (LFSR) encoder is a feedback structure: compute feedback = data_in XOR the TOP (last) parity register, then shift each parity stage from its lower neighbor while injecting feedback*generator_coeff via GF(2) XOR — not a normal add/carry. The feedback term must be a blocking assign (computed first) inside the clocked block so the SAME cycle's shift uses it, while all parity stages use non-blocking assigns so they update from the OLD stage values in parallel (mixing blocking feedback with non-blocking taps is the correct idiom; making everything blocking corrupts the shift). Reset must clear every parity register and valid_out, and valid_out should track the qualified enable&valid_in of the accepted symbol.

For a single-module edit/lint task whose context supplies other modules as SEPARATE files compiled alongside the edited file, emit ONLY the edited module; never inline a copy of a sibling context module — a duplicate module definition triggers an iverilog 'already declared' elaboration error (exit 2). Prompt hint here: intra_block 'should be excluded from the review' i.e. it stays its own untouched file.

In a Reed-Solomon or any GF(2^m) remainder LFSR the generator coefficients MULTIPLY the feedback symbol in the field; they are never XORed into it. XOR-with-the-polynomial is the GF(2)/CRC idiom, and on a symbol-wide datapath it produces parity that looks plausible and simulates cleanly, so a self-written testbench will confirm it. The canonical two-parity update is: fb = data XOR p_high; p_high' = p_low XOR (g1 (x) fb); p_low' = g0 (x) fb, where (x) is the field multiply. Use the first symbol out of reset as a free structural probe: with a monic generator whose lowest coefficient is the field identity, the low-order parity after one symbol is the data symbol ITSELF. If your first-symbol low parity differs from the data symbol by a fixed constant, you have XORed a coefficient where a field multiply belongs. Separately, treat prose that says 'the coefficients are XORed' in a symbol-wide code as under-specified rather than as a licence to XOR — bit-level XOR and field multiply coincide only when every coefficient is 0 or 1.

A LIFO/stack uses ONE shared top-of-stack pointer (not the separate head/tail of a FIFO): write stores at memory[ptr] then ptr++, read must fetch from memory[ptr-1] then ptr-- (the top element is one below the write pointer). Guard every mutation with the full/empty flags so overflow/underflow leaves memory and pointer untouched, and register the status side-flags: error must be sampled at the clock edge only when an enable hits an already-full/empty stack (so a legal fill/drain doesn't glitch it), and valid must be one-cycle-delayed to match the registered data_out (asserted the cycle the read result actually appears, else the checker samples stale data).

FIFO/ping-pong lesson: registered next-pointer comparison ((ptr+1)%D==other_ptr) makes full/empty assert one clock LATE and conflates full vs empty (pointers start equal). Draft's full asserts one cycle late, pushing the TB into its extra-cycle compensation path and de-aligning the exact-DEPTH drain so empty lands one cycle past the window. Rule: track occupancy with a count register or an extra pointer wrap/MSB bit so full/empty are unambiguous and asserted on the exact fill/drain cycle.

For a 2D sliding-window / border-extension extractor, out-of-range must be resolved PER-AXIS independently: compute row-source and col-source with the mode's rule (clamp/mirror/wrap/pad) applied separately to the row overflow and the column overflow, then index buffer[resolved_row][resolved_col]. A common bug treats "any overflow" as one condition and pads/zeroes the whole cell, which corrupts cells where only one axis is out of range while the other is valid (e.g. mirror gives 0x484d4d, not a padded value). Also: index the border math on the raw unbounded sum (row_start+row) using a signed/int intermediate, since the small NBW_ROW/NBW_COL start ports will wrap if the arithmetic is done at port width.

For block/line-code decoders (e.g. 64b/66b), decode is a two-level dispatch: FIRST branch on the sync header (framing bits) — an invalid header must raise ONLY the sync-error flag and force data/control outputs to zero, never the decode-error flag; SECOND, within the control frame, branch on the type field against an exact whitelist of legal codes, raising the decode-error flag (not sync-error) for any unlisted type. Keep these two error conditions on separate flags and separate causes. Build each output word by concatenating fixed control-character constants and sliced input data byte-lanes in the MSB-to-LSB order the spec's table lists, matching the per-lane control-output mask bit-for-bit; and register all outputs behind the valid strobe to honor the specified 1-cycle latency (hold prior output when valid is deasserted, async-reset to zero).

In a block line code (64b/66b and relatives) the payload of a control or mixed block is NOT a row of whole data bytes. Every control lane carries a narrow code field (7 bits in 64b/66b) that must be looked up in the control-code table to yield the 8-bit character — the all-zero code is the IDLE character, not the error character — and ordered-set lanes carry their own narrow code field. As a consequence the data lanes are not byte-aligned in every block type: a data lane's bit offset inside the payload depends on how many narrow code fields precede it. When a spec table writes a block type's output as a mnemonic tuple such as {E7..E0} or {I,I,I,I,D,D,D,Q}, it is naming the lane TYPES, not fixed character constants: hard-coding a character for a control lane is right only when the payload happens to carry that lane's code, and slicing data lanes at fixed byte boundaries is right only for the block types with no narrow field ahead of them. Derive every lane's bit offset from that block type's field layout and run every control lane through the code table.

A "fix the latch inference" task means every conditional path must assign every output: the true fix is an explicit else branch (or default assignment) that drives the spec-mandated idle value (here all-zero) when the enable is deasserted — not merely holding the previous value. Naive authors leave the else implicit, which infers a latch/holds stale data and corrupts downstream; register the output in a clocked block where reset, active, and idle branches each assign a defined value.

In a table-driven line/block encoder the block type field is a function of the decoded CHARACTER LANE PATTERN (which lanes hold idle / start / terminate / error / ordered-set / data), never of the raw per-byte control mask. A spec table that shows one control-mask value per row is showing one CONSISTENT mask for that row, not a lookup key: the same mask legitimately selects several rows (a terminate character in a lane is still a control character, so an all-ones mask can select a terminate row as well as the all-control row), and different masks can select the same row. Encode in two steps — classify each byte against the legal control-character set first, then match the resulting lane pattern against the table. Treat the table as the COMPLETE legal input domain: if any control-flagged byte is not a legal control character, or the lane pattern matches no row, the block is out of domain and must emit the spec's defined invalid output (typically the mode's sync header with an all-zero body), never a best-effort encoding of whatever bytes arrived.

A lint-cleanup task must fix each named class of warning WITHOUT altering the design's functional behavior: remove unused/undriven signals, give every register a reset value, move purely-combinational math into always_comb so the clocked block infers no latch, and resolve width-mismatch by an EXPLICIT sized cast (e.g. 16'(wide_sum >>> shift)) rather than silent truncation. Critically, preserve every original arithmetic detail — the accumulation, the fixed-point >>>N scaling that brings the wide multiply-accumulate back to output width, and any saturation branch — exactly as written; a lint pass that "cleans up" by changing the transfer function or dropping the shift is a functional regression, not a fix.

For a LINT clean-up of clocked RTL, enforce assignment-type consistency by intent: every state/output update inside an always_ff must use non-blocking (<=); blocking (=) is legal ONLY for local loop indices/temporaries (e.g. `int i` in for-loops), and the two must never be mixed on the same sequential storage — mixing causes simulation-vs-synthesis race/mismatch. Separately, prune every declared-but-unassigned/unread signal and unused parameter (dead nets, extra localparams, unused array ports), since dangling drivers are the other canonical lint class. The trap: leaving a genuinely-used loop iterator blocking looks like a violation but is correct, so classify by whether the LHS is persistent state, not by the operator alone.

For a LINT-cleanup review task, the deliverable is functionally-identical RTL with only the flagged violations removed — never a rewrite. Two recurring traps: (1) never mix blocking (=) and non-blocking (<=) assignments to the same variable across a design's sequential logic — use <= consistently in every clocked always block (blocking only in initial/combinational); (2) delete every truly-unused parameter/package/typedef the linter flags, but preserve parameters that are used indirectly (e.g. to size localparams or derive other params) since removing those breaks elaboration. Change nothing that alters behavior or port/parameter interface visible to the testbench.

A byte/word-granular LSU must split each memory access into a word-address plus a two-bit byte offset and drive the bus with a per-transaction byte-enable mask (be_first for the low word, be_second = shifted mask for the crossing word), never the raw effective address. Latch the request context (aligned-word address, type, offset, byte-enables, sign-extend flag) at accept time so a multi-cycle FSM transaction stays stable while the input changes. Critically, only NATURALLY-aligned single-transaction loads get sign/zero-extended-and-shifted data forwarded to writeback; every misaligned/multi-transaction access (and even a single-transaction access that isn't naturally aligned) must forward the raw byte-masked memory response word per transaction — mixing these up is the trap. Also gate the writeback valid/data strictly on dmem_rvalid_i in the correct GNT state, and zero ALL bus outputs whenever dmem_req_o is deasserted.

For a multi-stage streaming MAC/accumulator, size the accumulator to exactly 2*DWIDTH + $clog2(N) bits (product width plus carry growth for summing N terms) and gate every pipeline register on a valid signal that has been delayed to match its own stage, so counting, accumulation, and valid_out all track the true datapath latency (first result at N+1 cycles). The critical trap: gapped valid_i must freeze all stages (hold state, advance nothing), and at the window boundary the accumulator must restart by loading the in-flight product rather than zeroing — otherwise the first sample of the next window is dropped and back-to-back windows lose one term.

To embed an m×n operation inside a fixed N×N datapath (m,n ≤ N), zero-pad into a block-diagonal placement: put the active m×n block in the top-left and drive all out-of-range rows/columns to 0, so the unused lanes contribute nothing to the result rather than injecting X/garbage.

For combinational 2D matrix transforms on a flattened bus, address every element with one consistent row-major mapping, element = bus[((r*NCOL)+c)*DATA_WIDTH +: DATA_WIDTH], and build each rotation purely by re-indexing the SOURCE (padded) array rather than chaining registers: 90° CW = out[i][j]=src[N-1-j][i], 180° = src[N-1-i][N-1-j], 270° = src[j][N-1-i]. Pad non-square inputs into an N=max(ROW,COL) square first so a single square index scheme covers all angles. Key trap: when the prose padding/orientation description conflicts with the golden reference model, the index formula must match the reference's actual element placement (and its input-vs-output stride difference IN_COL vs OUT_COL), not the ambiguous English, or every vector mismatches by a transpose/flip.

On a FLATTENED matrix port the geometric words in a padding spec ("bottom-right portion", "top rows and left columns are zero") only acquire meaning once the (row,col)->bit-slice order is pinned, and the two common flatten orders map the very same sentence onto OPPOSITE corners — so a prompt that names a corner but never names the bit order has not actually specified the placement. Resolve it toward the offset-free placement, where input element k lands on padded element k and the pad occupies the far end, and say so in a comment: the alternative injects a constant pad offset that survives every rotation, and because each angle re-indexes that offset differently, the result is a per-angle row-shift for one angle and a column-shift for another, which is exactly the signature a vector comparison reports (identical data, displaced zeros). Anchor the choice with fixed points you can check blind: for a square input the padding step must be the exact identity, and the pass-through/no-rotation mode must map input element k to output element k for every k. If you keep the far-corner reading instead, you have implicitly chosen the other flatten order and must index EVERY stage (pad, transpose, and all rotations) in that same order consistently.

For an area/latency PPA-optimization task on an FSM datapath, functional equivalence is the hard gate — so bound every index/counter register by its true algorithmic maximum (here merge-sort indices never exceed 2*N, so ADDR_WIDTH=clog2(2*N)+1 replaces 32-bit `integer` comparators) and drop dead states to shrink the state register (removing a terminal DONE state cuts 3 state bits to 2 AND saves exactly the required 1 cycle). The latency cut must come from folding the terminal state's work into the prior state so `done` and the result appear the SAME cycle a checker expects; and outputs should be driven combinationally as a fixed concatenation of the memory array rather than through a copied output register + mux network, eliminating cells/wires without changing done/state timing.

In a spec-driven datapath (bit-slice ALU + PC + LIFO + decoder) the dominant correctness risk is signal-polarity and enable-combination discipline, not the arithmetic. Implement each control exactly as the spec defines its polarity and combining rule: an active-low port must be inverted before use, and composite enables follow the stated boolean (e.g. register-write enable = rce OR ~r_en, mux-select = rsel AND ~r_en, output-drive = oe AND ~oen). Encode each mux's select-to-input mapping to the literal table given (they are NOT uniform across muxes), and keep the purely combinational blocks (adder, muxes) feeding the clocked blocks (PC reg, aux reg, result reg) so the multi-cycle latencies for registered operations (e.g. PUSH=2, POP=3) fall out naturally while unregistered fetches appear same-cycle. Guard stack pointer inc/dec with the full/empty flags to prevent over/underflow.

An iterative learning/compute engine driven by a microcode-ROM address counter must sequence one full pass through fixed micro-steps then return to an explicit idle/"waiting" state, and must LATCH the operands (applied_x1/x2) at pass start so the datapath uses a stable snapshot while inputs drift on the bus — this keeps the iteration index paired one-to-one with each applied input vector even when a vector is held for many clocks. Combinational intermediates (e.g. y_in = bias + x1*w1 + x2*w2) should be computed into a temp variable and then registered so the same value feeds both the registered output and the thresholding decision in one step. Convergence/"stop" is detected by comparing the current per-iteration deltas against the previous iteration's deltas (registered), not by an epoch cap; and a control-input change (new gate_select) must fully re-initialise weights/index/flags and re-arm the first-vector capture.

When a design has distinct sequential phases (e.g. train-then-test) driven by a testbench that samples outputs at fixed time checkpoints rather than via a handshake, the DUT must synchronize its internal phase advance to the SAME event the TB uses to sequence stimulus (here input-change detection via registered *_q comparators, and a fixed SLOT_CYCLES tick counter) so that phase-N results land on checkpoint-N regardless of how long each stimulus is held. Keep signed arithmetic honest: sign-extend narrow signed operands (threshold) to the full accumulator width before comparing, size the product/accumulator wide enough to avoid truncation (12-bit yin from 4-bit inputs), and expose a stored expected-vector table so the internal self-check compares against a golden reference the same cycle it registers the computed output.

When a spec says a new phase EXTENDS an existing microcode sequencer, that phase's iteration RATE is part of the contract, not a free implementation choice: build it as additional states of the SAME sequencer so one iteration consumes the same number of clocks one iteration of the existing phase does, and let it advance on the same event that sequences the stimulus. A private free-running FSM that retires one iteration every few clocks races ahead of a checker that samples a fixed delay after the phase begins, and every later checkpoint compounds the skew. Diagnostic signature to recognize immediately: at the checkpoint the internal index/state is several iterations AHEAD of the one the checker names, and the values it is showing are internally self-consistent (its own expected-vs-actual comparison matches) — that combination means a cadence bug, never an arithmetic bug, so do not go re-deriving the math. Verify arithmetically before coding: (checkpoint delay in clocks) divided by (clocks per iteration) must land on the iteration the spec's waveform labels at that checkpoint. Note that exposing a per-phase state output does NOT imply the phase may own an independent clock-rate sequencer.

For a threshold/overflow flag on a synchronous counter, compare the NEXT value (COUNTER + 1), not the current COUNTER, against the limit inside the same clocked block — a nonblocking COUNTER<=COUNTER+1 has not yet updated, so testing the old value latches overflow one cycle late (off-by-one). Also, in a single-phase MMIO decode the write address/data and the counter increment are evaluated in the same always block using the current registered enable, and read data (HRDATA) must be purely combinational off the address so the bus master samples the live register value with no wait state.

For a memory-mapped start/stop control of a counter or datapath, decide and implement WHICH clock edge produces the first count after a start/resume write. If the enable flop and the increment live in the same clocked block and the increment is gated on the REGISTERED enable, the write edge sets the enable but does not count, so the datapath resumes one clock later than a reference that gates on the enable's NEXT value (registered enable OR the current start decode, minus the current stop decode). The difference is invisible while the counter free-runs and surfaces only on a resume-after-stop or resume-after-overflow sequence, exactly where a directed test samples the counter on fixed edges after the write. Related discipline for the same class: AHB-Lite separates the address phase (HSEL/HADDR/HWRITE) from the data phase (HWDATA) by one clock, so a slave that decodes HADDR and HWDATA in the same cycle mis-times or drops writes; register the decoded address and write-enable in the address phase and apply HWDATA on the following cycle. Whichever convention you pick, apply it identically to every control register so start, stop and threshold writes all land on the same edge.

For an MMIO timer/counter with a level interrupt, the match-triggered interrupt must be edge-detected (pulse only on a NEW match, using a sticky "already-matched" flag) rather than set continuously while count==match, and a write to the status register must clear it with PRIORITY over the set path in the same cycle — otherwise a held match perpetually re-asserts the interrupt and the write-to-clear never wins. Also register writes take the low bits of the wider AXI data ({16'd0,field} on read, wdata[15:0] on write), reset is synchronous, and reads are combinational with a default-0 case so undecoded addresses return 0.

For sum-of-products modular arithmetic (matrix multiply mod N), size every intermediate accumulator to the full un-truncated worst case (each W-bit product needs 2W bits; a sum of k products needs 2W+ceil(log2 k) bits) BEFORE taking the modulo, then make the final narrowing back to the field width an EXPLICIT cast on the mod result (which is provably 0..N-1). This avoids silent bit-truncation on the products/sums and eliminates width-mismatch lint warnings, while keeping the modulo operand widths matched so the % never truncates.

For a multi-cycle modular linear-transform (matrix-vector mod-N) datapath, size the dot-product accumulator to the pre-reduction worst case (here max element 25*25*3=1875 needs 11-12 bits, not 5) and defer the mod-N reduction until AFTER the full sum is accumulated; reducing per-term or truncating to the output width mid-sum gives wrong residues. Latch all operands at start into registers so the datapath is stable across the FSM stages, and align the registered-output latency exactly to the documented cycle count with 'done' asserting the same cycle the result becomes valid (checker samples on done), holding done until the module is re-armed.

For an iterative multi-cycle compute engine (sort/search/accumulate) whose spec dictates a per-phase latency budget, decompose the FSM so each specified "1 clock cycle to do X" maps to exactly one distinct sub-state, and let the state advance ONE step per clock — do not collapse setup/access/compare-shift/insert into fewer cycles or fold them combinationally, because the testbench samples the result at a spec-derived cycle count and will read stale/premature data if your latency differs. Keep the array in a register file, use non-blocking assignments so a shift (array[j]<=array[j-1]) and the pointer update happen atomically per cycle, drive out_data and done together in the terminal output cycle, and preserve the exact port list / async-reset discipline of the original module.

Non-restoring division needs a partial-remainder register one bit wider than the operands (W+1) so the accumulator's MSB acts as a true sign bit; each iteration shifts A:Q left, then adds M when A<0 or subtracts M when A>=0 (not the restoring "always subtract, restore on fail"), sets Q[0]=~sign(A_new), and after the last of exactly W iterations applies the mandatory final correction A += M when A is still negative before A yields the remainder. Skipping the +1 width or the final sign-correction is the classic bug that produces an off-by-divisor remainder.

Any field-programmable non-volatile memory — one-time-programmable, fuse-based, multiple-time-programmable, antifuse — separates two operations with different electrical needs. READING needs only the core supply. PROGRAMMING needs a SEPARATE supply that is sourced from OUTSIDE the die, sits ABOVE the core voltage, and enters through a dedicated terminal. Nothing on-die produces a voltage above the core rail, so the programming supply can never come from the internal power grid; it has to arrive on a package pin or a wafer-probe pad. Treat this as a property of the storage mechanism rather than a vendor option: two unrelated programmable-memory IP families characterised on one process — one process-native, one third-party — specify it identically, both externally supplied and both above the core rail. So when an input instantiates such a memory AND describes programming control (a program request, an address, data, a busy/done handshake), the design is stating it intends to burn the array: ask where the programming supply enters, and capture it as a first-class terminal in the pin/pad table and as its own rail in the power-intent layer, kept distinct from the core rail. Capture the read path too — it needs the core supply alone, so a design that only reads a pre-programmed array legitimately has no such terminal, and the two cases must not be conflated. Nothing in a digital flow observes this gap: simulation, elaboration, synthesis, timing, DRC and LVS are all clean because the logic is entirely well-formed. It first appears at bring-up, on silicon, as an array that will not accept a burn.

When hardmacro_supply_intent.py / ip_integration_check.py flag IP_MACRO_SUPPLY_RAIL_UNDECLARED / IP_MACRO_SUPPLY_UNDECLARED (WARNING, #309) — a hard macro's OWN LEF/Liberty types a pin as a supply/programming terminal (USE POWER, or a Liberty pin(){direction:input;...} on a rail meant for field-programming) and nothing in L21_POWER_INTENT.fields.hard_macro_supplies[] accounts for it — the terminal exists on real silicon and needs SOME binding; the WARNING cannot be resolved by guessing a rail, and it must never be resolved by narrowing what the detector looks at. The two-step diagnostic that turns the WARNING into a cited, defensible binding hypothesis in one pass instead of several rounds of re-discovering the same two documents: (1) read the macro's OWN datasheet DC Operating Conditions / electrical-characteristics table and note, for EACH functional mode the macro supports, how the flagged pin's required voltage relates to the core supply (identical to it in some modes, elevated above it in others — the read-vs-program voltage split the sibling lesson above already documents for this same ic_class); (2) separately read the RTL that instantiates the macro to determine which of those modes the integration can EVER reach — a control input hardwired to a constant, with a comment explaining why, proves a mode is permanently unreachable in this build, which is a stronger claim than 'the current testbench does not exercise it'. The rail binding follows from the INTERSECTION: the datasheet's stated relationship for the one mode (or mode set) the RTL can actually enter. Cite the exact datasheet table/row AND the exact RTL tie-off (file:line, the constant, the comment) in the proposal — a binding with no citation to both sides is a guess wearing this procedure's shape, not the procedure. Where it lands once accepted: a hard_macro_supplies entry {master, pin, rail} (or {..., integration_gap: true} if the answer is still genuinely undetermined) in L21_POWER_INTENT. This is a DIAGNOSTIC ACCELERANT, not an authorization shortcut: the specific rail choice stays macro-specific and mode-specific — never lift a derived answer into a general rule ('tie unbound programming pins to the core rail') applied to a different macro, or to the same macro in a build that reaches a different mode set. Writing the resulting L21 entry for a real/tapeout-track design still requires an explicit human sign-off on the proposal before it is committed; this procedure only changes what the reviewer is handed — cited evidence instead of an open question.

A mutually-exclusive one-hot control decode can be safely rewritten as a flat one-hot AND-OR sum-of-products (each output = OR of the AND-terms whose select bit is hot) for area optimization — this is logically equivalent to a priority/case decode ONLY because the selects are guaranteed one-hot; do not apply it when more than one select can be high.

'Registered output' means EXACTLY one clock of latency: the result of inputs sampled at edge N is visible at edge N+1 — do not add a second register stage 'for safety'; a double-registered done/valid arrives one cycle late and every downstream sample slips by one. 'Combinational' or 'same-cycle' means ZERO added cycles. When a spec states a cycle count ('result after N cycles', 'done asserts in the cycle the last element is processed'), count from the edge that SAMPLES the start/enable, and emit a status/valid flag in the SAME cycle its data is valid unless the spec explicitly separates them. When the spec is silent on latency for a computed output, one registered stage is the conventional default — pick it, state the assumption in a comment, and keep every output of the block consistent with the same convention.

When a spec pins an exact output latency ('the outputs and the valid flag appear N clocks after <completion event>'), budget the registered stages between that event and the port and count them literally. The trap that costs the extra clock: a status flag that is BOTH registered AND used as the FSM's own transition condition costs TWO clocks, not one — one edge to set the flag, another before the state register can observe it. A chain of separate registered flags (done -> state change -> result latched -> valid) reads naturally and overshoots the stated budget by one or two; collapse the intermediate flags, or drive the state transition from the combinational completion condition and register only the port. This matters most when valid is a one-cycle strobe, because the data registers move with it: a checker sampling at the stated cycle then reads the reset value, so an ALL-ZERO capture is the signature of a late strobe, not of a broken decoder — confirm by re-simulating the decode standalone before touching the datapath. Also remember many cocotb checkers read a signal in the same delta as the clock edge and therefore see the PRE-edge value, which spends the whole budget you have.

A one-cycle valid strobe never implies a one-cycle data payload. When a spec sentence lumps the data outputs into the 'valid will be HIGH for one clock cycle' clause, read it as fixing the STROBE's alignment and width, not the payload's lifetime: latch the result, pulse only valid, and HOLD the data outputs until the next operation actually begins (or reset) — never add an else-arm that returns the payload to zero right after the pulse. Checkers overwhelmingly sample at end-of-stimulus plus a fixed slack, i.e. at or after the strobe cycle, so held payload passes under every sampling schedule while pulsed payload passes only if the checker lands on the exact cycle. Signature to recognise: every functional test reads all-zero outputs while the reset test passes AND a standalone re-simulation shows the correct value alive for one cycle — that is actively cleared payload, not a broken decoder; count the hold window before touching the datapath.

A word-wide (WIDTH bits/clock) LFSR must be built by UNROLLING the single-bit recurrence: in a combinational block iterate a temp copy of the register WIDTH times, each iteration computing feedback = reg[tap]^reg[0], emitting that bit, then shifting the temp — and only the final unrolled state is clocked into the register once per cycle. Do NOT clock the register WIDTH times or you produce one bit/clock. For a PRBS checker, run an INDEPENDENT local LFSR (same seed/evolution) and XOR it against data_in for error detection; do NOT load data_in into the shift register (that would corrupt the reference sequence and create a startup transient). Match the exact bit-order/tap convention (feedback into MSB vs LSB, tap index) stated in the spec, since it changes the emitted sequence.

For a word-wide (WIDTH bits/clock) LFSR/PRBS block, the packing of the parallel word is a SECOND independent convention besides the tap-index origin, and a byte-exact checker fails outright on the wrong choice. Class default: the FIRST serially-generated bit of each cycle lands at bit 0 (LSB) of data_out — time order runs LSB→MSB — unless the spec shows an explicit packed-word example; treat prose like "the feedback bit becomes the MSB" as describing the SHIFT-REGISTER insertion end, never the output-word packing. Two implementation guards: (a) never rely on an ascending `[0:W-1]` helper wire assigned onto a descending `[W-1:0]` port — that mapping silently bit-reverses the word; index data_out[i] explicitly per emitted bit. (b) Self-check before delivery: flatten your own consecutive output words LSB-first into one bit stream and assert the single-bit recurrence o[m]=o[m-TAP]^o[m-LENGTH] holds across word boundaries — a wrong packing (and a wrong tap origin) both break it, a correct design satisfies it.

A parallel-prefix (Brent-Kung/Kogge-Stone) adder must compute sum[i] = p[i] ^ c[i] where p=a^b is the HALF-sum (XOR only, NOT a^b^cin folded in) and c[i] is the carry INTO bit i, with c[0]=carry_in and the prefix recurrence c[i+1]=g[i]|(p[i]&c[i]). Two class traps: (1) carry_out is c[32] (the carry out of the MSB), NOT g[31] or a truncated bit — size the carry vector W+1 wide; (2) index alignment — sum uses c[31:0] (carry-in of each bit), never c[32:1]. The hierarchical tree only reduces logic depth; it must produce bit-identical carries to this ripple recurrence, so verifying the flat recurrence form guarantees correctness.

When a parameterized array of identical submodules is required, drive it with a genvar `generate for` loop that instantiates the child inside a named `begin:label` block and indexes an unpacked wire/reg array (`[0:N-1]`) for the per-instance outputs; wire the output from the correct boundary index (here `[NEURONS-1]`). Watch the register-update trap in the leaf cell: a "hold previous value unless enabled" element must have NO `else` after the `else if (enable)` branch in the sequential block, so the flop retains state when disabled — adding an else (e.g. clearing) would silently break the retain-on-idle semantics — and reset must stay in the async `negedge rst_n` branch.

A ping-pong (double-buffer) design must gate write and read against a per-bank "frame ready" flag, not raw pointer positions: write only into the active bank while its ready flag is clear, read only once it is set, and toggle buffer_select at the pointer's wrap boundary (write toggles on fill, setting that bank's flag; read clears the flag when drained). Empty = active bank not-ready, full = OR of both bank-ready flags. Because the dual-port SRAM output is registered (one-cycle read latency), capture data_out with a synchronous register on the read cycle so the checker samples the addressed word, and keep pointers/flags/data_out all in the async-reset sequential block using non-blocking assignments.

On a block/ping-pong claim interface feeding a stream, the claim/activate output must be RELEASED ON THE SAME CLOCK EDGE that completes the final beat: in the send state, when (valid && ready) fires and the beat counter shows this beat exhausts the block (count+1 >= size, or the captured last flag), clear the claim output in that very branch — never route the release through a later compare-then-release FSM state. Hidden checkers assert the interface's end-state (claim and strobe both 0) immediately after observing the last handshake, with zero grace cycles; a 1-2 cycle detour is invisible to a real FIFO but fails that sample. Also read the spec's edge-case examples as live input→output constraints: an example pairing "fifo ready = 0" with "activate = 0" is satisfiable at all times by qualifying the registered claim with the live ready input, which independently covers the checker that drops ready right after the last word. Symptom signature to recognize this class: every payload/last/user comparison passes and the test fails only on a final-state assert of a claim or strobe output.

For a priority arbiter checked against a golden scoreboard, the winner-selection RULE (effective-priority formula, saturation, AND the tie-break direction) must be bit-identical to the reference model, not merely "reasonable": scanning indices 0..N-1 with `if (pending[i] && eff >= sel_pri)` deterministically makes ties resolve to the HIGHEST index, whereas `>` would pick the lowest — a silent mismatch the checker catches. Compute effective priority combinationally over the full pending set (kept separate from the registered FSM so the winner is stable), and use a comparison width wide enough to hold the boosted/saturated value before truncating to the id field. Equally load-bearing is honoring the exact multi-cycle handshake latency the testbench samples (trigger→valid latency and the ack→drop→re-assert cadence): a registered-output controller must land each output on the precise cycle the scoreboard windows it.

A priority interrupt controller must arbitrate over the *effective* pending set (pending AND mask) with a fully-initialized best-priority accumulator (best_pri=all-ones, lowest value wins, ties to lowest index) so masking and priority both bind; and it must clear on ack the interrupt that was actually *presented* to the CPU (a registered serviced index), not the currently-arbitrated one, so a higher-priority request arriving on the ack edge cannot cause the wrong bit to be cleared. Synchronize async requests through a flop before OR-ing into the pending register, and derive cpu_interrupt from a registered "effective-pending exists" flag gated off during ack (and one cycle after) to produce clean idle→pending edges and a gap between back-to-back services.

In a request/ack interrupt (or arbiter) controller, the bit cleared on ack must be the selection the CPU actually SAMPLED, not the current combinational winner. Because the CPU reads interrupt_idx just after a clock edge (the pre-edge value), you must register the selected index/eligibility (idx_clear_q/elig_clear_q) one cycle and clear THAT indexed pending bit — clearing the live sel_idx races the arbiter and can drop the wrong source. Sequence the pending update as: clear-acked-bit FIRST, THEN OR-in the freshly synchronized new requests, so a same-cycle re-request is never lost; combine this with a registered request synchronizer plus a one-cycle rise delay and post-ack recovery cycle to give the deterministic >=2-cycle request-to-interrupt latency such handshakes need.

For a level-style request/acknowledge interrupt line, treat the acknowledge as terminating the request in the SAME cycle it is observed, not on the following edge. Drive the CPU-request output from the current arbitration/servicing state (combinationally, or registered off next_state) so that it already reads low on the cycle ack is high; a controller that clears it with a non-blocking assignment inside `if (ack)` leaves it asserted across the entire ack cycle, and a scoreboard that samples request and ack together reads that overlap as a second, spurious request for an interrupt it is already retiring. Keep the serviced-vector clear, the pending-bit clear and the request drop in one cycle so no window exists where the CPU sees both signals high. The same discipline applies to the re-assert edge: if another interrupt is still pending, the next request must rise on the cycle after the ack, so build the ack path as arbitrate-and-reload rather than as a return trip through an idle state.

When an interrupt controller has both a one-shot "start processing" trigger and a multi-entry pending set, the trigger arms the SET, not a single entry: latch it and hold it until the pending mask drains, rather than clearing it the moment the FSM leaves idle, or the second and later requests of a burst are stranded forever with valid low. Pair that with a fast path from the completion state straight back to arbitration whenever the remaining pending mask is still non-zero, so valid re-asserts on the cycle after the acknowledge instead of walking idle->calculate->prepare again. Checkers for this class are written as a standing invariant — valid must be high whenever anything is pending — so both failure modes (a trigger consumed per interrupt, and multi-cycle dead time between services) show up as the same "no interrupt active while N pending" report; when you add pipeline states for priority calculation, make sure their latency is hidden behind a still-asserted valid rather than exposed as a gap.

A hidden scoreboard drives only the ports its tests exercise; a documented feature port it never touches (a per-line enable/mask, an override bus) floats at X for the entire run. Any AND/OR of such a port into the request-capture or state-advance path turns the pending bits X, and every `pending != 0` or `if (pending[i] && ...)` guard downstream then evaluates FALSE in four-state simulation — the FSM never leaves idle and the standing liveness invariant (grant/valid high while anything is pending) fails at its very first sample, even though the identical RTL is fully live the moment the mask is actually driven. Confine each optional feature input to the outputs that report that feature: a mask belongs in the missed/masked bookkeeping the spec names, and in arbitration ELIGIBILITY only if the spec explicitly says masked requests must never be serviced; keep the raw request-to-pending capture and the leave-idle guard mask-free. This is the missing precondition on the earlier 'arbitrate over pending AND mask' rule of this class: qualify with the mask only where a floating mask cannot veto liveness, or the design deadlocks under the very testbench that grades it.

A request/interrupt line cleared by a consumer ack has a TWO-SIDED contract, and the tight side is re-assertion: (1) never high while ack is high — mask the pin combinationally with !ack; (2) the moment ack is low, if any eligible source is still pending the line must be high again within the next cycle — do NOT insert recovery/idle states between services, and keep the whole request->line path to at most two clock edges (one sample/edge-detect stage ORed into pending at that same edge; grant decoded from registered pending, never re-registered). Cycle-accurate monitors budget about two cycles from 'any pending & !ack' to the line being high, and read every extra synchronizer or recovery stage as a missing interrupt. Never prescribe added pipeline/recovery cycles as 'safe' craft — added latency is only safe when the spec itself quotes a synchronizer depth or wait-state count.

While the interrupt/request line is asserted and not yet acknowledged, re-arbitrate the presented index/vector every cycle to the current best eligible pending source — checkers commonly assert `presented_idx == best(live pending set)` on every cycle the line is high, so a selection latched at grant time reads as a wrong ID the moment a better-priority source arrives mid-service. Lock the presentation only when the spec explicitly says the selection is held until ack. Live presentation is compatible with correct ack-clearing: clear pending[index the consumer actually sampled at the ack edge] (register the presented index for the clear), never pending[live winner at clear time].

For a processor/CPU-core class design, an L10 case is sometimes a BOOT-LATENCY property rather than an instruction-execution oracle: "N cycles after reset release, the design has performed its first bus access / instruction fetch". Recognise this SHAPE by grammar in the case's own stimulus/expected text (a reset-release reference + a first-activity reference + an explicit "N cycle" bound), never by the case's name. It is derivable WITHOUT an instruction-set model: extract the design's own declared N-cycle bound from that same text (treat an informally-qualified "typical" number as an inclusive upper bound, not a hard ceiling, and say so), then pick the DUT's own structurally-detected bus-activity OUTPUT (the Wishbone-family cyc/stb/req/valid vocabulary — standard bus terminology, never a chip literal) as the observable "first activity" signal. Drive reset, release it, count clock edges, and FAIL if the activity signal never asserts within a small margin over the bound, or asserts later than the bound. DEFER (leave the honest substance-floor testbench) when the case-text shape, the clock, the bus-activity output, or the explicit numeric bound is missing — never invent one. Verified worked example: a RISC-V bit-serial CPU-core reused-IP integration's `reset_n_cycle_instruction` case — first bus-activity observed at clock cycle 3 against a declared max of 10, confirmed by compiling and simulating the generated oracle TB against the real RTL (genuinely PASSes at the true latency, genuinely FAILs when the declared bound is tightened below it).

An L10 case conditioned on an OPTIONAL Plugin-selectable feature — text carrying an explicit parenthetical marker such as "(若 Plugin 選 <token>)" / "(if the plugin selects <token>)" — applies ONLY when THIS build actually selected that feature axis. Before demanding a functional-TB golden for such a case, check the design's OWN `declaration.json` (or equivalent structured Phase-2 config) for an affirmative record of the referenced token (a WORD-BOUNDARY match — a short token like 'M' or 'C' must never be matched as a bare substring, which would trivially hit almost any JSON blob). If declared, the case is a real requirement and needs a genuine golden the normal way. If `declaration.json` is silent or absent, the gate cannot confirm applicability: never hard-FAIL a possibly-unselected optional feature, and never fabricate a golden for hardware that may not exist — WAIVE the case as a distinct, reviewable "conditional feature selection undeclared" gap (not the same capability-gap class as a generic missing-oracle deferral, since the root cause here is a missing DECLARATION). Verified worked example: a RISC-V core's plugin_m_mul_div / plugin_zicsr_csr_access_timer_irq / plugin_c_16_bit_compressed cases — direct RTL inspection proved the instantiated core implements none of M/Zicsr/C, and no declaration.json was ever produced to record that decision, so fabricating goldens for them would have tested hardware that does not exist.

In a radix-4 (modified) Booth signed multiplier, each 3-bit overlapping group must be recoded to a SIGNED multiple of the multiplicand (0, ±X, ±2X) computed on a value already sign-extended to the FULL product width, and only THEN arithmetically left-shifted by 2*group_index — with signed operands and arithmetic shift (<<<) so negative partial products keep their sign through the shift and the summation tree. The classic bug is generating the ±2X/−X term or the alignment shift at the narrow operand width (or unsigned), which truncates the sign/overflow bits and yields wrong products; recode-then-sign-extend-then-shift-then-accumulate in the correct order is what makes the class correct.

A multiport register file's memory array must have exactly ONE synchronous driver: mux the BIST-generated writes and the normal write port inside a single always_ff on the primary clk (BIST writes when test_mode, normal writes otherwise), never a separate gated/enable-latched write clock — a gated clock lags clk by a delta and drops single-cycle wen pulses. Reads are zero-latency combinational (a value written on a prior edge is visible the same cycle rad/ren are presented), and BIST must be a full write-all-then-read-all march (separate WRITE then READ passes over every address, comparing each read against a deterministic address-derived pattern) before asserting bist_done, with normal read/write/collision logic forced off during test_mode.

REFINES the existing register-file-with-bist entry. A memory BIST's pattern is not private state: the array it fills is read back through the FUNCTIONAL port after test_mode drops, so the pattern is externally observed and is part of the module's post-BIST contract. Pick a pattern that is non-zero at EVERY address and distinguishable from the reset / never-written value. An address-derived counter violates both at address 0, where the array reads back exactly like an uninitialised location, so any post-BIST check on the low addresses cannot distinguish 'BIST ran and left its pattern' from 'BIST did nothing' — and address 0 is the address such a check almost always uses. When the spec says only 'a known pattern', prefer a replicated non-zero byte from the conventional RAM-BIST checkerboard family (a constant identical at every address, which also keeps the read-phase compare independent of the address counter); if the array must return to a defined state instead, clear it explicitly on the way out of the read pass rather than leaving march values behind. Also deassert bist_done when test_mode drops, so the status bits describe the current mode.

When a spec mentions a reset without stating polarity or synchrony, take the convention from the SIGNAL NAME first: an _n/_b suffix (rst_n, resetn, nreset) means active-LOW, a bare rst/reset means active-HIGH. Put the reset in the sensitivity list (asynchronous assert) only when the prose says asynchronous / 'immediately' / 'regardless of the clock'; otherwise default to synchronous sampling at the active clock edge. Reset must return EVERY architectural register AND every declared output to its stated reset value (0 when unstated) so a sample taken right after deassertion reads defined values. When the spec says a control/clear input 'clears all outputs' with no timing qualifier, the asynchronous-assert form is the robust superset — it satisfies both an immediate-sampling and an edge-sampling consumer, while the synchronous-only form fails the immediate one.

A directed-rounding unit's per-mode decision must be driven purely by the guard/round and sticky bits plus the sign, never by inspecting the fractional remainder value: round-up = f(roundin, stickyin, sign, lsb). The traps to avoid are (1) RNE ties must break to even, so round-up = roundin & (stickyin | lsb) — a bare tie (round set, sticky clear) only rounds up when the current LSB is odd; (2) RUP rounds up only for positive inexact values (~sign & (roundin|stickyin)) and RDN only for negative ones, i.e. directed modes are sign-gated; (3) since incrementing is just in_data + 1 within the same WIDTH, carry-out/overflow (cout) is exactly the all-ones-input AND round-up case, and inexact is roundin|stickyin independent of whether a round-up actually happened. Keep it combinational with a default (unsupported mode) that truncates.

A rounding unit's overflow behavior is a per-mode convention axis, not a single rule: a reference may WRAP the increment with carry-out in the direction away from the operand's sign (ceiling on a positive value) yet SUPPRESS the increment entirely — output held, no carry — when a sign-matching directed mode (floor on a negative value) would overflow the all-ones magnitude. A spec sentence like "cout=1 if the rounded value exceeds the representable range" permits both wrap and suppress, so treat the all-ones input under each directed mode as an explicit convention decision: enumerate {wrap+cout, suppress+hold} per mode in the design notes, and self-test every mode at the all-ones input, because that single vector flips out_data, cout AND the round-up indicator at once. Absent any worked example covering it, record the chosen convention rather than assuming symmetry across modes.

When parallelizing a per-element stateful encoder (RLE, counters, accumulators) into N independent lanes, replicate ALL state as arrays inside a genvar for-loop and drive each lane purely from its own index — never share a counter/prev register across lanes — then pack lane outputs into the flattened bus with a consistent stride (here W=$clog2(DATA_WIDTH)+1, slice [(i+1)*W-1 : i*W]) so the counter width covers the max value inclusively. Correct RLE termination is a two-condition emit-and-restart: assert valid/output the ending run when EITHER the input changes OR the counter reaches the maximum, and on that same cycle reset the counter to 1 (not 0) since the current sample already belongs to the new run; getting the max-length boundary to restart at 1 while emitting the completed run is the trap naive authors miss.

A streaming run-length counter must emit-on-event, not emit-continuously: pulse `valid` for exactly one cycle on the two distinct events — a value transition (data_in != prev) OR the counter saturating at its max run length — and drive it low otherwise. Compare the CURRENT count against the parameter-derived max (with the counter width sized as $clog2(DATA_WIDTH)+1 so DATA_WIDTH itself is representable without overflow), and on either event latch the just-completed run into run_value while restarting the counter at 1 (not 0) since the current bit already belongs to the next run. Use the registered prev_data_in for both edge detection and data_out to keep valid/run_value/data_out phase-aligned on the same clock edge.

For a sequence-gated (multi-step unlock) register bank, model unlock as an explicit FSM whose state advances only on CONSECUTIVE matching operations and re-locks on ANY deviation: a wrong code, a write/read to a non-sequence address mid-sequence, or a read that interrupts the two unlock writes must all fall through to the LOCKED state. Because the sole clock is the strobe (i_capture_pulse) with async active-low reset, evaluate state transitions and register storage in one clocked block; guard both reads and writes with the unlocked state, make special/reserved addresses (0,1) write-only (read as 0), and default o_data_out to 0 on every write and every disallowed read so stale data is never exposed.

For a shift-and-add sequential multiplier, the accumulator and the shifted multiplicand must both be the full 2*WIDTH product width before shifting (zero-extend B to 2*WIDTH, then `b_ext << cnt`), otherwise high-order partial products get truncated and the product is wrong for large operands. Equally load-bearing is honoring the exact stated latency contract: the design commits to a fixed cycle count (here WIDTH+2 = 1 latch + WIDTH accumulate + 1 register/pulse), so the step counter must be wide enough ($clog2 of the max count, not WIDTH), Product must be registered on the SAME cycle valid_out pulses (else the checker samples stale data), valid_out is a 1-cycle default-low pulse, and a `start` busy flag must gate new valid_in so mid-computation inputs cannot corrupt the run.

A random-access indexed write into a register array where the index advances by exactly one each accepted item is equivalent to a ring-counter-addressed serial-in-parallel-out (SIPO) shift collector; the SIPO form removes the index decoder and is the canonical compact implementation when writes are strictly sequential.

In a mode-selected line-code encoder, every encoder variant must be computed as its own independently-registered signal every cycle (running state like alternating-invert toggle, running parity, and prev-sample edge detectors keep advancing regardless of which mode is selected) and the mode selector must be a purely combinational mux over those registered outputs — do NOT gate the per-encoder update logic by mode, or stateful encoders lose history when temporarily unselected. Also detect x/z on the serial input with the 4-state case-equality operator (===, not ==) since == against x/z yields x and would never flag an error, and place enable/output-disable gating in the final combinational mux (forcing serial_out=0) rather than freezing the internal state registers.

In a source-synchronous serializer/deserializer, transmit a gated data-valid strobe alongside the serial line (serial_clk active ONLY while a real bit is on the wire) and have the RX shift/capture bits only when that strobe is high — this keeps both ends in one clock domain and avoids gated-clock sampling races. Critically, because the last serial bit is written into the RX register on a clock edge, its value is not visible until the NEXT cycle: assert 'done' and latch the assembled parallel word one cycle AFTER the final bit is captured (pipeline a last_bit flag), or a checker sampling data_out coincident with the last-bit strobe reads a stale/incomplete word. Also size bit counters to the max width (here 7 bits for up to 64) but index the storage array with only the needed low bits.

For a serial-parallel / bit-serial multiplier (parallel multiplicand x, serial multiplier y one bit per cycle, serial product p) that carries a stated clock-frequency target, do NOT author the behavioral form (accumulate `acc + (y?x:0)` then shift-and-emit each cycle): that places a full DATA_WIDTH-bit carry-propagate adder in the register-to-register path and misses an aggressive clock — measured on a 32-bit design it failed a 100 MHz / 10 ns sky130_fd_sc_hd target by ~24 ns worst slack. Instead use the SYSTOLIC carry-save array (Lyon bit-serial): hold the accumulator in redundant (sum, carry) form as two per-bit registers; each bit i is a single full-adder `{carry[i],sum[i]} = (x[i]&y) + s_hi[i] + creg[i]` where the >>1 accumulator shift is pure wiring (`s_hi = {1'b0, sreg[size-1:1]}`), then register `sreg<=sum; creg<=carry` and emit `p<=sum[0]`. The critical path is ONE full-adder (register-to-register) independent of width, so it closes timing at any reasonable clock while producing the IDENTICAL LSB-first serial product (low DATA_WIDTH bits = x*y mod 2^DATA_WIDTH) with the same 1-cycle output latency. Same result on the same design: systolic form met the 100 MHz target at +3.82 ns slack, DRC-clean and LVS-matched. General rule: when a bit-serial datapath has a clock target, redundant carry-save state beats a per-cycle carry-propagate accumulator.

To author a functional-testbench GOLDEN for a serial-parallel / bit-serial arithmetic datapath (a parallel operand, a bit-serial operand and a bit-serial result on an N-bit datapath computing p = a OP b mod 2^N), do NOT copy the spec's prose 'expected' description into the vector as though it were a value, and do NOT read the product back from the DUT to 'confirm' it — either fabricates coverage. Instead COMPUTE the golden INDEPENDENTLY from the design's DECLARED function (product = a times b, sum = a+b, ... from the L2/L7 closed-form operator) as an N-bit constant, then verify the DUT's SERIAL output stream against it using the three framing facts the datapath is FREE to choose and therefore DECLARES in its interface contract (declaration.json bit_order / latency_cycles / integer_encoding, or the equivalent RTL-header 'DECLARED CHOICES' block): bit_order (LSB- vs MSB-first, for the serial operand AND the result), output latency_cycles, and integer_encoding (two's-complement is bit-identical to unsigned mod 2^N, so the output bit-pattern golden is the same either way). Choreography: drive the parallel operand held; stream the serial operand one bit per clock per the declared bit_order; sample the serial result at each clock; reassemble the product window [latency, latency+N) per bit_order before an === compare. These framing facts tell the oracle HOW to place the golden, never WHAT it is: a DUT that computes the wrong product fails at any declared framing, so the oracle stays falsifiable. When bit_order/latency are NOT declared the serial framing is not derivable — DEFER (leave the substance-floor testbench) rather than guess, because a fabricated golden is worse than an honest gap. Corner operands to always include: 0, 1, all-ones/MAX, MIN (signed), and -1. Same convention generalizes across the operator (+ - * & | ^ << >>) and across a fresh design of the same interface shape — it is keyed on the shape, not on any one design.

In a serial TX/RX link with a parity-integrity check, the receiver must recompute parity over the fully-reassembled data word (^data_reg) and compare it against the transmitted parity bit as a STICKY/latching error flag that settles a cycle before the sampling edge of `done` — a single-cycle pulse aligned exactly with `done` risks being read while still resolving. The transmitted parity must also be carried on a continuously-held (combinational, no clocked overwrite) path so it stays valid through the whole frame and propagates straight into the comparison; and reception/validation should be gated on the RX-side bit counter reaching the expected width, not on a fixed delay, so the check fires only after all bits arrive.

Width-parametric parity: compute parity across the FULL parametric data width (a reduction XOR over the whole word) and capture it at the correct pipeline stage. Computing parity from a shifting register at the wrong cycle mis-times the capture, and hard-coding the default (e.g. byte) width makes parity and parity_error wrong for larger widths — parametrize the parity datapath by the data-width parameter and verify it at each supported width.

Serial-to-parallel deserializer collecting N bits into a word with a REGISTERED valid output: shift the incoming bit in at the LSB while the register shifts left (`data <= {data[W-2:0], din}`) so the first-received bit lands in the MSB (MSB-first). For the completion strobe, size the bit counter to N+1 terminal states (count 0..N, not 0..N-1): shift on counts 0..N-1, and assert the REGISTERED dout_valid on the dedicated terminal count N — i.e. ONE cycle AFTER the Nth bit is shifted in, when the full word is stable — as a one-cycle pulse, then return to 0. A registered output inherently lags one cycle, so asserting valid the SAME cycle as the Nth shift races the consumer; the extra terminal state also cleanly re-synchronizes the counter when the upstream valid strobe deasserts irregularly around the last bit. Gate the counter/shift on the input valid and clear the counter when it deasserts so each frame starts aligned.

In a multi-order sigma-delta/noise-shaper error-feedback loop the accumulator paths grow width stage by stage (each integrator adds A1/A2 guard bits), and the quantizer error feeds combinationally back into the earlier stages. Every operand in these add/sub expressions must be sign-extended (replicate the MSB, not zero-pad) to the exact width of the wider accumulator, or width-mismatch truncation silently corrupts the noise shaping and lint flags it. The 1-bit PDM output is the inverted sign/MSB of the quantizer decision registered each clk-enable cycle; dither is a self-seeding LFSR added only to the quantizer input. Also purge dead code that lint catches: unused localparams and implicit timing controls.

For an area-reduction/logic-restructure task the golden constraint is bit-exact functional AND latency equivalence to the reference, so every algebraic rewrite must be provably identity, not approximate: signed saturating add is done with ONE (W+1)-bit sign-extended sum and clamp when bit[W]!=bit[W-1] (never a separate MAX/MIN comparator chain), and a two-sided magnitude threshold |s|>=T is folded to one comparison via m = s ^ {W{s[W-1]}} with the off-by-one correction (compare against T-1 when s<0, T when s>=0) instead of computing s>=T OR s<=-T with a real negation. Redundant thresholds also collapse: OR of several |s|>=Ti reduces to |s|>=min(Ti). Keep FSM states, register count, and the exact cycle on which sum_ready/outputs assert unchanged.

When chaining a registered producer (SIPO shift register that completes on 'done') into a downstream registered consumer (CRC generator), you must pipeline-align the data: feed the consumer the parallel word delayed by exactly the consumer's own register latency (here two clocks via parallel_out_q1 -> crc_data) so its output validity coincides with 'done'; naively wiring the live shift-register output makes the checker sample a stale/partial word. Also match reset polarity/synchronicity per port (the shift core uses async active-low reset_n while the CRC uses a synchronous active-low rst), and drive combinational encode/syndrome logic (Hamming) from unregistered nets so the current word is encoded without an extra cycle of skew.

A skid buffer must decouple the combinational ready/valid pass-through from the registered stall path: assert o_ready = ~buffer_full and drive o_data/o_valid as a mux (held beat when full, else pass input through combinationally), then capture into the skid register ONLY on the stall event (i_valid & ~i_ready while empty) and release it when downstream becomes ready. The naive trap is registering the whole datapath (adding latency) or making ready depend combinationally on downstream ready (creating a ready->valid->ready combinational loop across stages) — a true skid buffer breaks that loop by having exactly one register-deep buffer that absorbs a single beat during back-pressure while keeping the empty-state ready purely a function of its own occupancy.

In a serial-shift-out FSM, enforce clear-over-fault-over-normal-state priority, make one-cycle status outputs owned by their explicit event/state, and prepare every externally sampled data/status signal BEFORE raising a generated clock/strobe. Use a PREPARE phase to select/drive the next bit and update bits-remaining/status, followed by a STROBE phase that changes only the generated edge; nonblocking updates to data/status in the same arm that raises the strobe are observably late/racy. Verify with an edge monitor that snapshots data/status at the generated rising edge and proves they do not change in that timestep.

For clock-domain time-based generators, derive slow time bases (ms/us ticks) as single-cycle strobe pulses from a down-counter loaded with (CLOCK_HZ/1_000_000)*PERIOD_US cycles, and use those strobes as clock-ENABLES on the single system clock — never gate/divide the clock itself. Nested timers must only advance on their parent strobe (decrement duration on the ms tick, toggle the square wave on the us tick), size counters/localparams with $clog2(DELAY+1) to avoid width truncation, derive busy purely combinationally from counter!=0, and generate a one-cycle done by registering busy and detecting its falling edge (busy_d & ~busy) so the completion pulse lands the exact cycle activity stops.

In a cache/TLB with a combinational associative lookup but a registered (synchronous) fill, you must pipeline-latch the request that missed: capture the looked-up virtual_address AND its fetched entry into registers, then install them one cycle later at the replacement slot — because by the time the fill's write-enable asserts, the live input address has already advanced, so writing `virtual_address` directly caches the wrong tag. Also drive hit/miss combinationally from the valid-bit + tag compare with a safe default of miss=1/hit=0 (overridden inside the match loop), invalidate all valid bits on both reset and flush, and advance a round-robin replacement index only on an actual write.

When a lookup/translation spec states that the result is available 'on the rising edge of clk' after a miss, that edge count is the binding contract and it outranks the prose that also describes a ready/valid handshake with the backing store. Build the refill so the fill write-enable is a combinational function of the miss and the fetched entry a combinational function of the index, and let the control FSM's states run alongside the fill rather than in series with it. Every stage you insert costs exactly one edge — a registered `ready` from the memory model is one, a separate FETCH state that waits for it is another, the tag write is a third — and because the lookup output defaults to the miss value, a checker sampling on the next edge sees the reset/zero result rather than a late-but-correct one, so an over-serialized refill looks like a dead lookup instead of a latency error and gets debugged in the wrong place. Count edges from stimulus to observable output before writing the control FSM, and reserve a multi-state handshake for a backing store whose latency the spec actually quantifies.

A hidden/whitebox harness commonly binds hierarchically by the design's OWN internal signal names under the top-level instance. Deliver the design as ONE FLAT module under the stated top name — never wrap the logic inside an inner sub-module the harness cannot see, and keep the internal signal names intact rather than renaming or re-hierarchizing them.

A whitebox/cocotb harness binds DUT members by name, and its reach is wider than the port list: it binds module PARAMETERS and internal registers just as readily. Expose every spec-stated numeric bound or configuration constant — a counter's terminal value, a max/min, a depth, a width — as a NAMED `parameter` on the top module, taking the identifier stem from the spec's own words, instead of inlining the literal; a bound that lives only as a literal is unbindable and crashes every test with 'no child object named X' before a single functional check runs, and naming it costs nothing in area or timing. Keep every backtick-quoted spec identifier verbatim on top of that. Know the asymmetry when you hedge: a second name for an OUTPUT is free (append an aliased output, continuously assigned), but a second name for an INPUT is not — an extra input the bench never drives floats to z and poisons any expression it feeds, so a reset the harness binds under a different NAME can never be rescued by aliasing. That makes the reset identifier the single highest-cost naming decision in the design; take it from the spec exactly as written and change nothing about it.

A white-box harness binds by hierarchical NAME; a name it cannot find aborts the whole test before any functional check, so a naming miss costs the entire score while a wrong computation costs one vector — budget care accordingly. When a spec states outputs in single-letter or heavily abbreviated form (`w`, `b`, `q`, `y`), treat the identifier as UNDERSPECIFIED: keep the spec's spelling on the port and additionally declare an inert observer net for the conventional decorated spelling of every OUTPUT (`wire [W-1:0] w_out = w;`), restricted to simulation-graded deliveries (an unused net is a finding under strict lint — guard with `ifndef VERILATOR when a lint service may run). Inputs cannot be rescued this way — an undriven input floats — so when a spec offers two spellings of an INPUT, spend the disambiguation effort there.
